videos.title: Who Bought All the RAM in 2026? 🧠
videos.description:
Why are phones and laptops getting more expensive in 2026? The AI memory shortage, explained.
RAM (DRAM) prices are surging as AI data centres buy up memory.

TrendForce says DRAM contract prices rose about 80% in Q2 2026 and about 40% in Q3, with roughly 20% more forecast for Q4 — about three times the start-of-year level if that holds. videos.title: The Coin That Trapped Coca-Cola 🥤
videos.description:
Why did a Coke cost 5 cents for 70 years? The nickel Coke, explained.
How a 1899 bottling deal and nickel-only vending machines froze Coca-Cola's price.

In 1899 two lawyers got Coke's bottling rights with the syrup price fixed permanently. Coke tied its brand to five cents, and its vending machines took a single nickel — the next coin up, a dime, would have doubled the price. Coca-Cola asked the US Treasury for a 7.5-cent coin, and its boss even raised it with his hunting buddy, President Eisenhower. The answer was no. Inflation won, and the nickel Coke was gone by 1959.

videos.description:
Fake FBI "recovery" calls: why scam victims get scammed a second time.
How the IC3 impersonation / fund-recovery scam works, and the one rule that stops it.

After a scam, a second call comes: someone posing as the FBI or its Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) says they can get your money back for a small upfront fee. The FTC warns that recovery scammers buy lists of people who've already been scammed. The FBI (PSA, July 2026) warns of AI deepfake videos of an FBI leader sending victims to a spoofed IC3 site. The real IC3 never contacts you first and never asks for payment to recover lost funds.

videos.title: De Beers' $6.8B Problem 💎
videos.description:
"A Diamond Is Forever": how De Beers made diamonds feel rare, and why lab-grown diamonds are breaking the spell.
Why diamonds resell for so little, explained.

De Beers once controlled most of the world's diamond supply. In 1947 its ad agency, N.W. Ayer, wrote "A Diamond Is Forever" — and "forever" discouraged resale, so few people learned how little a used diamond fetches. Later ads pushed "two months' salary"; the share of US brides with a diamond ring rose from about 10% to about 80% (Al Jazeera). Lab-grown stones now cost up to 80–90% less, and Anglo American has written De Beers down by $6.8 billion since 2023.

videos.title: Someone Bought the Eiffel Tower? 🗼
videos.description:
The man who sold the Eiffel Tower: Victor Lustig's 1925 con, explained.
How a fake government letterhead and a luxury hotel fooled a Paris scrap dealer.

The Eiffel Tower was built on a 20-year permit. In 1925, con man Victor Lustig posed as a government official, invited scrap-metal dealers to the Hôtel de Crillon and said the state would secretly sell the tower for scrap. Dealer André Poisson paid, plus a bribe, and Lustig vanished. Poisson was too embarrassed to go to the police, so Lustig tried the same con again — this time a dealer called the police and he fled. Parts of the story come from later retellings.

videos.title: Stolen in 2017… With a Wheelbarrow? 🪙
videos.description:
The Big Maple Leaf: a 100 kg gold coin stolen from Berlin's Bode Museum with a wheelbarrow, and why its "$1 million" face value was the least valuable thing about it.

In March 2017, thieves climbed in from the railway tracks beside Berlin's Bode Museum and took the Big Maple Leaf, a 100 kg coin of 99.999% gold made by the Royal Canadian Mint. Its face value: one million Canadian dollars. Police put the gold at over $4 million at the time. Investigators believe it was cut up, melted and sold; three men were convicted in 2020 and the coin was never found. At gold's November 2026 price, 100 kg is worth about $13 million.

videos.title: Why Your Eggs Cost More Than Mine 🥚
videos.description:
Dynamic pricing explained: why the same eggs in the same store can show five different prices.
Personalised and algorithmic pricing: Instacart's price tests and AI airline fares.

Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that Instacart showed nearly three in four grocery items at more than one price in an experiment; a dozen Lucerne eggs from one Safeway in Washington, D.C. showed $3.99, $4.28, $4.59, $4.69 or $4.79. Instacart ended its item price tests on 22 Dec 2025. Delta has said AI helps set fares on about 3% of its domestic flights, with plans for up to 20%; Delta says it doesn't target individuals with personalised fares. Before a big purchase, compare the price on another app, device or in the store.

videos.title: The Free Trial Trap 💳
videos.description:
Free trial auto-renew: why a "free" trial needs your card, and how companies profit when you forget to cancel.
Subscription traps, hard-to-find cancel buttons, and the Amazon Prime "Iliad" case.

When a free trial ends, the card on file is charged and the plan renews automatically. The US Federal Trade Commission accused Amazon of enrolling people in Prime without clear consent and making cancellation hard; internally the cancel flow was nicknamed "Iliad". Amazon denied wrongdoing but in September 2025 agreed to pay $2.5 billion to settle — a $1 billion civil penalty and $1.5 billion in customer refunds. The fix: set a reminder the day you sign up, and check your statement for charges you don't recognise. Not financial advice.

videos.title: The Job That Pays You… Then Robs You 💸
videos.description:
Task scam explained: the "get paid to like videos" job that ends with you paying them.
How app-optimisation and product-boosting job scams work, and the one rule that beats them.

It starts with an unexpected text or WhatsApp message. You like videos or rate products in sets of 40, an app shows your earnings climbing, and small early payouts make it feel real. Then a "double task" asks you to deposit your own money, usually in crypto, to unlock your earnings. The balance was never real. The FTC counted about 5,000 task-scam reports in all of 2023 and about 20,000 in just the first half of 2024. BBB Scam Tracker puts the median task-scam loss in 2025 at about $2,300. The FTC's rule: never pay to get paid.

videos.title: Why America Killed the Penny 🪙
videos.description:
Why the US stopped making the penny: each one-cent coin cost almost 4 cents to make.
The end of the US penny, and why the nickel loses money too.

In 2024 the US Mint spent about 3.69 cents to make each penny. Pennies had been made since 1793. The Treasury placed its final order for penny blanks in 2025, and the last circulating pennies were struck in Philadelphia on 12 Nov 2025. The nickel costs about 13.78 cents to make and is still being produced. More than 114 billion pennies are still in circulation, and they remain legal tender.

videos.description:
Fake FTC call scam: "Your phone number is linked to a crime and will be deactivated."
How the government-impersonation call moves you from a fake official to a fake police officer to a "security deposit".

On 22 Oct 2026 the US Federal Trade Commission warned about callers posing as FTC officials who say a phone in your name is running scams overseas. They read a fake badge ID, threaten to deactivate your number, transfer you to a fake police officer, ask for your ID and secrecy, then claim you're under arrest unless you pay a "security deposit". The FTC says real employees never ask for money, threats to disconnect your phone are a scam, and requests for secrecy are always a scam. Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

videos.description:
Are Black Friday deals real? Why most "discounts" are the same price you could pay any other time.
The "was" price trick, countdown clocks, and why prices often drop again after the sale.

Consumer group Which? tracked 175 products at eight big UK retailers from May 2024 to May 2025. 83% were the same price or cheaper at least once outside the Black Friday sale period. videos.title: Infinite Money at the Bottom of the Sea 🌊
videos.description:
Rai stones of Yap: the giant stone money that worked even after one sank to the bottom of the sea.
How stone money on Yap shows what money really is.

On the Pacific island of Yap, money took the form of rai — huge carved stone discs, the largest about 3.6 metres wide and around 4 tonnes. Most were quarried on Palau, roughly 400 km away, and brought back by sea. Big stones were rarely moved; ownership changed by everyone agreeing who owned them. One stone sank on the way home, and the islanders still treated it as existing and kept trading it. Today most of our money is also just numbers that everyone agrees on.

videos.title: How Newton Lost His Fortune! 📉
videos.description:
Isaac Newton and the South Sea Bubble of 1720: how the genius behind gravity lost money in a stock bubble.
Why even smart investors buy at the top.

South Sea Company shares rose from about £130 in January 1720 to over £1,000 by June. Newton sold most of his shares early at a profit, then bought back in at roughly double the price before the crash. Estimates of his loss range from about £10,000 to over £20,000, and historians still debate the evidence. The famous line about calculating the stars but not the madness of people is attributed to him but not confirmed. Not financial advice.

Fake payment screenshot scam: how a "Payment successful" screen can show a green tick when no money was sent.
How shopkeepers get fooled by fake UPI/payment apps, and the one check that stops it.

The Mali emperor's pilgrimage to Mecca and its effect on Cairo's gold price.

On his way to Mecca, Mansa Musa gave gold to Cairo's officials, emirs and treasury, and his party spent freely. videos.title: Was the Rupee Ever Worth $1? 💵
videos.description:
Was 1 rupee equal to 1 dollar in 1947? The rupee vs dollar myth, fact-checked.
Rupee to dollar history: 1947, 1966, 1991 and today's near-record low.

In 1947 the rupee was pegged to the British pound, and a US dollar cost about ₹3.31 — never ₹1. India devalued to ₹7.50 per dollar in 1966, and after the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis the rate passed ₹30 within a year. In May 2026 the rupee hit a record low near ₹97; on 29 Oct 2026 it traded around ₹95. A weaker rupee also makes Indian exports cheaper abroad. Not financial advice.

videos.description:
Digital arrest scam explained: a "police officer" on a video call says you're under arrest — and the only way out is to move your money.
How the fake video-call arrest works, and the one rule that beats it.

One woman in India lost about ₹2.5 crore (~$260,000) in a single week. In 2024, Indians reported over 1.2 lakh digital-arrest cases and lost ₹1,918 crore (over $200 million). Police and agencies do not arrest anyone over a video call, and they never ask you to transfer money. On 29 Oct 2026 India's Supreme Court said banks that miss red flags should compensate victims. videos.title: Why Your $100 Ticket Costs $130 🎟️
videos.description:
Drip pricing shows a low price first and adds mandatory fees at checkout (the $100 to $130 ticket is an illustration). In a large StubHub field experiment (Blake, Moshary, Sweeney & Tadelis; Marketing Science, 2021), users who saw fees only at checkout spent about 21% more and were about 14% more likely to buy. The FTC's Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees, in effect since May 12, 2025, requires live-event ticket sellers and short-term lodging to show the total price, including mandatory fees, up front; taxes and shipping can still be added later. Tip: compare deals on the final checkout total.

videos.title: Tulip Mania 1637: The Bubble That Wasn't? 🌷
videos.description:
Legend says that at the peak of 1637's tulip mania, a single Semper Augustus bulb cost as much as an Amsterdam canal house; its reported price rose from about 1,200 guilders in the 1620s to an asked 10,000 guilders. Bulbs were traded on paper contracts while still in the ground, often in taverns, and in early February 1637 an auction in Haarlem drew no bids and prices collapsed within the week. But historian Anne Goldgar (Tulipmania, 2007) searched the records and could not find anyone who went bankrupt because of tulips; much of the famous drama comes from Charles Mackay's 1841 book. Economist Earl Thompson argued the peak prices reflected contract terms rather than a true bubble.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #tulipmania #history

videos.title: Pay With a Gift Card? It's a Scam. Every Time 🎁
videos.description:
The FTC's rule of thumb: no real business or government agency will ever tell you to pay with a gift card. Scammers pose as the IRS, tech support or a utility about to cut your power, keep you on the phone while you buy cards (sometimes at several stores), then ask for the card number and PIN. With those, the money can be drained within minutes while you're still holding the card, and gift-card payments are hard to trace or reverse. Americans report losing over $200 million a year to gift-card payment scams (FTC Consumer Sentinel data). If someone demands one, hang up and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #scamalert #giftcards

videos.title: Why Zimbabwe Printed a $100 Trillion Note 💵
videos.description:
Zimbabwe issued a 100-trillion-dollar note in January 2009; on its first day it was worth about US$30. In mid-November 2008 monthly inflation was estimated at 79.6 billion percent (Hanke & Kwok, Cato Journal), about 98% a day, with prices doubling roughly every 25 hours. The government removed 25 zeros in three redenominations (2006, 2008, 2009) before suspending the currency in April 2009 in favour of the US dollar and rand. In the 2015 demonetisation, accounts were converted at US$1 per 35 quadrillion Zimbabwe dollars, about 40 cents for a 100-trillion note. Today collectors pay around $100 for an uncirculated one, more than it was ever worth as money.

videos.title: Charles Ponzi Promised 50% in 45 Days 💸
videos.description:
In 1920 Charles Ponzi promised Boston investors 50% in 45 days, supposedly by buying international postal reply coupons cheaply abroad and redeeming them in the US. It couldn't work at scale, so he paid earlier investors with new investors' money. He took in roughly $15 million in about eight months (estimates range from about $10M to $15M; National Archives cites ~$15M). After the Boston Post's investigation, the scheme collapsed in August 1920; investor losses of about $20 million are over $200 million in today's dollars, and the Post won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service. Ponzi served prison terms, was deported to Italy in 1934 and died in Rio de Janeiro in 1949.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #PonziScheme #history

videos.title: The $6.50 Popcorn Trick Might Be a Myth 🍿
videos.description:
Why is the medium popcorn priced so close to the large? It may be a decoy: an option that exists to make another one look like a bargain. (The $3 / $6.50 / $7 prices are an illustration.)

The famous evidence is Dan Ariely's account of an Economist offer (web $59, print $125, print + web $125): he reported 84% of his MIT students picked the combo, and only 32% once the print-only option was removed. But that was a classroom exercise, not real subscribers; two of Ariely's other papers have since been retracted over data problems, and larger studies (Journal of Marketing Research, 2014) found the decoy effect weak or absent in many realistic settings. The useful test: would you buy the large without the medium?

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #pricing #psychology

videos.title: Why Prices End in .99 (It's Not the Cents) 🏷️
videos.description:
Why do prices end in .99? The left-digit effect: we read prices left to right and anchor on the first digit, so $9.99 feels like "nine-something" rather than ten.

It shows up in big purchases too: in more than 22 million wholesale used-car auction sales, prices dropped by roughly $150–$200 at each 10,000-mile odometer mark (Lacetera, Pope & Sydnor, NBER). And in a retail field experiment by Anderson (Chicago) and Simester (MIT), a dress sold better at $39 than at $34, suggesting a 9 ending itself signals a bargain. Tip: round up before you decide.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #pricing #psychology

videos.title: Why Costco's Hot Dog Is Still $1.50 🌭
videos.description:
Costco's hot dog and soda combo has cost $1.50 since 1985. Adjusted for inflation it would be around $4.50 today, yet the price hasn't moved, and Costco sold more than 245 million combos in fiscal 2025.

It works as a loss leader: a deal so cheap it brings people in, and getting in takes a membership. In fiscal 2026 Costco earned about $5.9 billion in membership fees against roughly $9.2 billion of net income, so fees are about two-thirds the size of its profit. (The founder's "raise it and I'll kill you" line is the widely told story.)

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

#Shorts #Costco #pricing

videos.title: SEBI Barred 59 for This Stock-Tip Trap 📉
videos.description:
How a stock-tip "pump and dump" works: operators buy a small, cheap stock, a group fills with targets and profit screenshots, and once followers buy, the operators sell to them. The price falls, the group goes quiet, and victims get invited to a new one.

On 22 October 2026 SEBI cautioned investors about unregistered, invite-only WhatsApp groups that use planted members to fake profits. In a 2025 final order in a YouTube-driven pump-and-dump case (Sadhna Broadcast), SEBI barred 59 entities and ordered about ₹58 crore returned. Before trusting any tip, check the adviser's registration on SEBI's website. This is not investment advice. (The ₹500 target and profit screenshots shown are illustrative.)

videos.title: That 70% Off Was Never Real 🏷️
videos.description:
That "70% off" is only as real as the "was" price it's counted from. Before a sale, the crossed-out price can be pushed up, so ₹999 looks like a steal even if it sold for ₹999 all month.

India's amended e-commerce rules (notified September 2026, in force from 1 January 2027) require a discount to be shown next to the "prior price": the lowest price in the 30 days before the sale. EU rules already measure discounts this way, and in an EU check of 314 online traders around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, about 30% still displayed discounts incorrectly. Tip: check a product's price history before you trust the crossed-out number. (The ₹1,999 / ₹999 prices are an illustrative example.)

#Shorts #fakediscount #onlineshopping

videos.title: Milka Shrank 10%. Did You Notice? 🍫
videos.description:
Milka bars in Germany went from 100 g to 90 g in the same wrapper. That's shrinkflation: the price rise you don't see on the tag.

Why it works: in US store data (NielsenIQ, 2010–2020), a 1% price rise cut sales about 1.2%, but a 1% size cut hurt sales only about half as much. After a downsize, the price per unit rose about 12% on average. In 2016 Toblerone widened the gaps between its peaks, and in May 2026 a German court (Bremen) ruled the Milka cut misleading. The fix: compare the price per kilo, not the price tag.

Scenes are drawn illustrations.

videos.title: The real reason Western cars suddenly fell behind (and China is behind it)
videos.description:
Right now there's a brand-new electric car on sale for about $10,000, with four doors, fast charging and a spinning touchscreen, and Americans aren't allowed to buy it. Washington put a 100% tariff on it and then banned the software inside it too. Meanwhile, the average new car in America just passed $50,000. So how did a country that couldn't build a decent car 30 years ago end up building one so cheap and so good that the U.S. had to make it illegal?

Data sources: BYD annual reports and sales filings, China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM), IEA Global EV Outlook, Kelley Blue Book / Cox Automotive average transaction prices, U.S. Commerce Department and USTR tariff and connected-vehicle rules, Ford, GM, Volkswagen and Toyota earnings, Xiaomi and CATL press releases, and reporting from Reuters, Bloomberg, CNBC, WSJ and Financial Times.

We cover the joint-venture deal that gave China the playbook, how China became the world's biggest car exporter, BYD's rise from phone batteries to beating Tesla, the battery supply chain chokehold, Chinese development speed, the $10,000 BYD Seagull, Xiaomi's SU7, five-minute charging, the subsidies debate, the price war, America's tariff wall and the Mexico back door, and whether Detroit can fight back. We also explain why Ford's CEO called it the most humbling thing he'd ever seen.

Can Western automakers still catch up, or is it already too late? Let us know in the comments.

videos.title: Volkswagen Is Losing Everything: Porsche, Audi & Golf on the Brink
videos.description:
Volkswagen, the biggest carmaker in Europe, now wants to cut up to 100,000 jobs. Its CEO calls it "the most comprehensive realignment in the company's history," and four German factories have no confirmed future in the next decade.

What went wrong? Deliveries in China fell by more than a third in a single quarter, US tariffs are costing the group up to $5.7 billion a year, its software unit keeps losing billions, and operating profit fell by more than half in 2025.

In this video, we break down how the people's car went from a bombed-out factory to a global empire, the decisions that built the trap, from Dieselgate to the electric bet, and whether Volkswagen can still turn it around.

videos.title: How Nissan Destroyed a $30 Billion Empire
videos.description:
Nissan sold its own headquarters in Yokohama for about $640 million, then signed a 20-year lease to keep working inside it. Today it is closing seven factories, cutting 20,000 jobs, and just posted a net loss of roughly $3.5 billion, its second deep loss in a row.

How did it get here? A rescue in 1999 that became a business school legend, a volume-at-any-cost strategy built on discounts, the arrest and escape of Carlos Ghosn, a collapse in China, no hybrids for America, a failed Honda merger, and US tariffs that wiped out almost $1.9 billion in profit.

In this video, we break down how the strategy that once saved Nissan ended up breaking it, what CEO Ivan Espinosa is doing to fix it, and whether Nissan can survive on its own.

Do you think Nissan can survive without being sold? Let us know in the comments.

videos.title: Millions of Americans Are Going Back to Using OLD CARS — And Here's Why!
videos.description:
Something unexpected is happening on American roads.

While automakers keep pushing bigger screens, more software, expensive EV technology and increasingly complicated vehicles, millions of Americans are moving in the opposite direction.

They are keeping their old cars.

Some are repairing vehicles they planned to replace.

Others are deliberately shopping for cars from the 2000s and early 2010s instead of signing up for another expensive new-car loan.

And the numbers show just how big this shift has become.

The average vehicle on American roads is now approaching 13 years old, while nearly one in three light vehicles is at least 16 years old.

The first reason is simple: new cars have become brutally expensive.

The average new-vehicle transaction price climbed above $50,000 in 2026, while the typical monthly payment moved close to $800.

That is before insurance, registration, fuel, maintenance and parking.

For many households, repairing an old paid-off vehicle now makes far more sense than starting another six- or seven-year loan.

Even a $2,000 repair can look cheap compared with twelve months of $700 or $800 payments.

Then there is insurance.

Modern cars are filled with radar sensors, cameras, LED lighting modules and advanced driver-assistance equipment.

A minor collision can now require new electronics, calibration and expensive replacement assemblies.

Repair costs for newer cars can be dramatically higher, and insurance premiums reflect that.

Thousands of Americans are getting out of their pickup trucks in 2026 — not because trucks suddenly stopped being useful, but because owning one has become brutally expensive.

In this video, we break down why late-model Ford F-150s, Chevrolet Silverados, Ram 1500s and Toyota Tundras are showing up across trade-in lanes, online listings and used-vehicle auctions.

The first problem is the monthly payment.

The average new-vehicle payment reached around $770 in early 2026, but a well-equipped full-size pickup can move far beyond that once buyers add crew cabs, four-wheel drive, larger engines and popular technology packages.

For many households, the truck payment now feels like a second rent bill.

Longer loans make the problem look smaller without actually fixing it.

By September 2026, a record share of new loans in the cited credit data stretched beyond 72 months.

Seven-year financing may reduce the monthly number, but it keeps buyers in debt longer and increases the risk that they owe more than the truck is worth.

That is where negative equity becomes dangerous.

Some owners trying to trade down discover that the dealer will not offer enough to clear the remaining loan.

Rolling that debt into the next vehicle simply moves yesterday’s truck payment into tomorrow’s smaller car.

Then come the real ownership costs.

AAA’s 2026 study put the ownership and operating cost of a half-ton pickup at around $1.10 per mile — the highest category in its comparison.

Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xDStpwVAQCg

Indianapolis, in the 1950s. Two brothers, Frank and Donald Thomas, own an equipment company and build a flame broiler that can cook eight hundred burgers an hour. Instead of just selling the machine, they decide to open their own chain. They call it Burger Chef. It spread across the United States by opening in smaller towns. In 1968, the food giant General Foods bought it. Burger Chef had six hundred locations in thirty-nine states by then, and General Foods kept expanding it. By the early 1970s, it had more than a thousand restaurants. One account says only McDonald's had more.

videos.title: Seinfeld chain, $1.25m #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xDStpwVAQCg

Now the number from the start. On April 1st, 1999, the hot dog company Nathan's Famous bought the chain's trademarks, its recipes and its franchise agreements. The price was $1.25 million in cash. Put that next to the other chicken chain. McDonald's paid $173.5 million for what was left of Boston Market. The name that had been on a Seinfeld set went for about one hundredth of that. Both chicken chains collapsed in the same year, chasing the same dinner. When two fast growers build for one market, it is not the market that doubles. It is the number of empty tables. The story has a strange ending.

videos.title: A billion on itself #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r-HmUgGzZCY

Here is the number from the start. After spinning off CarMax in 2002 and selling its credit card bank in 2003, Circuit City had cash. Under pressure from shareholders, it spent almost $1 billion between 2003 and 2007 buying back its own stock, at an average of about twenty dollars a share. By the end of 2007, those shares were worth four dollars and twenty cents. The money that could have carried the company through a recession had gone, and the sales floor that once made it special had been cleared out twice to save a fraction of that sum. It gets worse from here. Circuit City could not find a buyer, and its creditors would not back a rescue.

videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Im2nMNecAz4

Here is the sentence from chapter 1. In the shareholder letter of May 2022, the new chief executive, Barry McCarthy, wrote this: "We have too much for the current run rate of the business, and that inventory has consumed an enormous amount of cash, more than we expected, which has caused us to rethink our capital structure." That is the filing. And the balance sheet behind it was $1.4 billion in inventory, up from $937.1 million a year earlier, almost entirely finished products. In the same quarter, the company wrote down $182 million in goodwill. It named softening demand, higher costs of inventory and logistics, and a sustained fall in its share price.

videos.title: A waiting list doesn't cut prices #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Im2nMNecAz4

Think about that. A company with a waiting list does not cut its price. You cut the price when the line gets shorter. Then on November 4th, it cut its forecast for the year. It now expected revenue of between $4.4 billion and $4.8 billion, down from $5.4 billion. The company pointed to demand tapering as economies reopened. The stock fell by roughly a quarter, and by about a third at one point, depending on which outlet you read. Foley told investors on the call, "our teams have never seen a more complex operating environment in which to guide our expected results this year." That is a founder describing his own forecasting.

videos.title: $660 each #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zOt9umO8EGw

To get paid, you had to earn under $110,000 and have worked for the company for at least a year. Spread over roughly 33,000 people, it came to about $660 each, though amounts varied. The worker group Rise Up Retail said the severance owed was closer to $75 million. The three owners' stakes were effectively wiped out, Bloomberg Law reported. They lost money too. But lenders were paid first, and the workers were far down the line. Afterwards, the name did not die. A company called Tru Kids bought the brand in 2018. Later, with a new owner, Toys R Us shops opened inside more than 400 Macy's stores. The giraffe was back. The superstores were not. Go back to the opening. 735 stores, 33,000 people, and a business that still sold more than eleven billion dollars of toys in its final full year.

videos.title: Fired for selling well #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r-HmUgGzZCY

In February 2003, Circuit City dropped commissions altogether. On one day, it fired about 3,900 of its highest-paid salespeople, with a plan to hire about 2,100 hourly workers in their place. McCollough said the switch would save about one hundred thirty million dollars in payroll that year. What did the sales floor learn from it? Tom Wulf said anyone still working in a store thought that if they were too successful, they would be fired for making too much money. "So there was no incentive anymore," he said, "to take good care of the customer." Alan Wurtzel agreed the costs had to come down. His complaint was the way it was done. "It was done secretly and behind their backs," he said, "and they walked into work one morning and were told they were out of work."

videos.title: The treadmill recall #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Im2nMNecAz4

On March 3rd, 2021, a six-year-old child died after being pulled under the back of a Peloton Tread+, the company's treadmill. The machine had a raised, slatted belt with a gap beneath the rear. On April 17th, the US Consumer Product Safety Commission publicly warned people with children or pets to stop using it. At that point it counted one death and 39 incidents. That same day, Peloton put out a statement saying the commission's release was, in its words, "inaccurate and misleading." Less than three weeks later, the company reversed. On May 5th, it recalled about 125,000 Tread+ machines.

videos.title: The bubble under the comics #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7dpDrldPPY8

The comics world was in a boom. Collectors were buying new issues in sealed bags, sure they would be worth a fortune. Marvel leaned right into it, with variant covers and foil covers. It bought the trading card maker Fleer in 1992, and a rival card company, SkyBox, soon after. In 1994, it bought a sticker company, Panini, and a comic distributor, Heroes World. Notice how much of that was spending, and how little of it was making a better story. Every purchase was a bet that the boom would keep going. A company that big needs the next buyer to show up every month, and nobody had asked who the next buyer was. Think about what that means. The comic boom was a bubble made of collectors, and not of readers. Marvel was selling to people who planned to resell. When those buyers stopped, there was nothing underneath. Shops that had stocked up for the boom went bust, and Marvel's comic and card sales fell with them.

videos.title: Spider-man for $7 million #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7dpDrldPPY8

In 1999, Marvel licensed the movie rights to Spider-Man to Sony Pictures. The price was reported at around $7 million, plus a small share of the film's revenue and toys. Fox took the X-Men, and its film came out in 2000. On May 3rd, 2002, Spider-Man opened in theaters. It made $114.8 million in its first weekend, the first film ever to pass $100 million in three days. It went on to make more than $820 million worldwide. So how much did Marvel see of that? A licence fee and a share. Sony got the movie. And for the next several years, that was how Marvel's characters made it to the screen, with other studios holding the main prize. If you were Marvel, you'd have noticed something about those numbers. The studios were making hundreds of millions off Marvel's own creations.

videos.title: The loan that bet on ten heroes #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7dpDrldPPY8

On April 28th, 2005, Marvel announced two things at once. A distribution deal with Paramount Pictures, covering 10 films. And a loan from Merrill Lynch for $525 million, spread over seven years. Here is how the loan worked, and it is why people called it a gamble. It was non-recourse. If the films failed, the lender could take the movie rights to the ten characters Marvel had pledged, including Captain America, Nick Fury and the Avengers. But it could not go after Marvel itself. Merchandise and comics income was kept out of reach. Look at what that left on the table. Spider-Man and the X-Men were already licensed to other studios, so they could not be pledged. Marvel was betting the heroes it still had, and it was not at all clear that anyone would pay to see them. If you're thinking this sounds like Marvel still had one foot in the grave, it did not.

videos.title: The loan it carried #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zOt9umO8EGw

Here is the part that matters. The three firms put in about $1.3 billion of their own money, according to Bloomberg's figures. The rest was borrowed. And in a leveraged buyout, the borrowing does not sit with the buyers. It is placed on the company being bought. The old debt, about $2.3 billion, stayed. The new debt joined it. Toys R Us, the thing that had been bought, now owed the money that was used to buy it. Think of it like buying a house with a mortgage, then handing the mortgage to the house. The house still has to cook, clean and keep the roof on, and now it has to pay the bank too. So the company had a new job. Before, it sold toys and kept the profit. Now it sold toys and paid the lenders first. Did that look like a problem to the owners? Probably not on day one. The chain was huge, and its sales were over eleven billion dollars.

In 2022, Bird's operating expenses were $447.6 million. Of that, $215.8 million was impairment, a write-down of goodwill and of vehicles, parts and deposits. The company around the rides cost almost twice its entire revenue of $244.7 million. In 2021, the pressure came from the other side. An impairment is an accountant admitting that something is worth less than the company paid for it.

videos.title: 28.8 days #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b8hGr54sSRM

Quartz, working from an analysis by The Information, found the average scooter there lasted just 28.8 days. That is about 100 rides. At 70 cents a ride, the typical scooter earned something like $65 to $75 over its whole life. The Information estimated the company lost $293 on each scooter it put out. The ride made money. The scooter lost money. That is the first line of the ledger. There is a caveat, and it matters. This was one city, over four months, in the first year, with scooters Bird had bought rather than built. Nobody outside the company could see the rest of the fleet. So treat the $293 as an estimate of what was happening in Louisville, and as the question every investor had to answer next: would the scooters get better?

videos.title: Pan am sold its building #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lf6Bjrjpcjc

In 1981, Pan Am sold the Pan Am Building in Manhattan to the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company for $400 million. It was reported as a record for a single building. The tower that carried its name above Grand Central became someone else's. And that wasn't enough. In April 1985, Pan Am agreed to sell its entire Pacific division to United Airlines for $750 million. That included 17 of its big jets and the routes they flew. The Pacific was the profitable part. It was more than a fifth of what the airline earned in 1984, when its total operating revenue was $3.3 billion. Here's the number from the start of this video. When that sale was reported, Pan Am had lost more than $1 billion since 1980. That was five years of losses, reported before the bomb at Lockerbie.

videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lf6Bjrjpcjc

On January 21st, 1970, the first scheduled 747 flight was meant to leave New York for London in the evening. An engine overheated. The airline had to find a substitute aircraft, and the jet finally left at 1:52 in the morning of January 22nd, with 332 passengers on board. It took 6 hours and 14 minutes. Remember that first night, because it was the start of a decade where things kept going slightly wrong. If you're enjoying this, subscribe. There are more collapses coming, told the same way. Trippe stepped aside as the jets arrived. Najeeb Halaby, a former head of the Federal Aviation Administration, took over in 1969, and William Seawell replaced him in 1972. So the new managers inherited the bet, not the man who made it. The 747 arrived just as the United States and Europe slid into recession.

videos.title: The $525 million order #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lf6Bjrjpcjc

On April 13th, 1966, a man named Juan Trippe signed an order for 25 Boeing 747s. The price was about $525 million. At the time, it was reported as the largest order for commercial aircraft ever placed. The 747 did not exist yet. It was a set of specifications. Trippe had asked Boeing for a jet more than twice the size of the 707, carrying more than 400 passengers, and he wanted it within three years. A fishing-trip story gets told about how the idea began, with Trippe asking whether Boeing would build it if he bought it. Treat that as a legend. The signed order is the record, and the order is what matters here, because everything after it was paid for by the people who had to fill those seats. And the order came with a condition. For six months, Boeing would hold back jumbo orders from Pan Am's competitors.

videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O4sREilQ3VM

Summer 2004. Blockbuster was finishing a divorce. Viacom, which owned 81.5 percent of its shares, planned to let go of the company completely. Before it did, Blockbuster would pay a special cash dividend of $5 a share. On September 3rd, it paid it. The total was $905.6 million. Where did that cash come from? Not from a pile in the vault. Blockbuster borrowed $650 million from banks and sold $300 million of bonds paying 9 percent. That's $950 million of new debt, to hand over $905.6 million. And who got it? Viacom's filing said it expected about $738 million of the dividend, tax-free.

videos.title: Nine in ten visits #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r-gzZDxXBbk

And then the number. On October 8th, 2018, Google's engineering chief for the project, Ben Smith, wrote on Google's blog: "The consumer version of Google+ currently has low usage and engagement: 90 percent of Google+ user sessions are less than five seconds." Read that again. A service with a claimed 540 million users, and nine in ten visits ended before you could read a headline. Whatever the signup count said, the visits said people were leaving at once. In the same post, Google said it had found, in March 2018, a bug that could have exposed about 500,000 accounts. The consumer version closed on April 2nd, 2019. This is the odd one in the group. Google+ never lost a crowd.

videos.title: $47 billion was never cash #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J35gsF7dNBo

Now look at what that $2 billion actually bought, in a deal that valued the company at $47 billion. One billion was new money into the company. The other billion was used to buy shares from existing investors and employees. And the price per share implied a total value of $47 billion. Do the sum. Two billion dollars on forty-seven is about 4 percent. A cheque for a small slice of the company set the price for all of it. That is how a valuation works. It is what the last buyer was willing to pay, multiplied by everything else. So the valuation was an opinion with a signature on it. The cash in the building was a different, much smaller thing.

videos.title: 12,400 different parts #shorts
videos.description:
Full video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WzF3Zyblt9o

But here's what the licences hid. By 2004, the company was making more than 12,400 different elements. Each odd part needed its own mould, its own box, and its own place in a warehouse. Nobody could easily say which ones paid for themselves. Think about what that means. A company can sell more every year and still lose money on each extra product, if it cannot see what each one costs. Sales go up. Cash goes down. The two lines cross, and nobody in the building has a single clean number that explains why. That is what an annual report means when it says growth was unprofitable. It does not mean nobody bought the toys. It means the toys cost more to bring to market than they earned. Jorgen Vig Knudstorp saw this from the inside.

videos.title: Zoella’s "12 Days of Christmas Advent Calendar" (Failed Holiday Endorsement) #zoella #celebrity
videos.description:
Zoë Elizabeth Sugg, also known by her online name Zoella, is an English media personality, entrepreneur, and author.

In 2017, ahead of Christmas, she released an advent calendar in partnership with Boots UK Limited. While this wasn’t just any ordinary Advent calendar, it was a 12-day one. 
The price was set at a whopping £50 (around $65 US Dollars). 

Now you may ask what was included in this for it to be very expensive, well… It came with the following:
Two cookie cutters, A small pack of confetti, seven stickers, 1 small, scented candle, A makeup purse, and a small notebook.

Critics and reviewers calculated the actual value of the items to be significantly lower than the £50 price tag, estimating them to be worth perhaps £20 total at retail, which is about $20 US Dollars. 

This led to accusations that Zoella (whose real name is Zoe Sugg) was exploiting her young and impressionable fanbase.

Following widespread backlash and negative reviews, Boots responded by reducing the price of the advent calendar by half, with Zoella herself later releasing a video stating she did not have the final say on the pricing.

#zoella #adventcalendar

On November 28th, 2008, a crowd of over 2,000 shoppers waited outside of a Walmart store in Valley Stream, New Jersey,y shortly before its opening at 5 am. 

As soon as the doors opened, the impatient crowd knocked down the employee, who was later identified as 34-year-old Jdimytai Damour, to the ground as he opened the doors. 

He was later rushed to a local hospital and pronounced dead later that day. 4 other people were hospitalized, including a 28-year-old pregnant woman who was also knocked down a short distance away from Damor.

The other 3 people taken to the hospital only suffered minor injuries.

Wal-Mart Stores Inc. in Bentonville, Ark., would later call the incident a “tragic situation” and said the employee came from a temporary agency and was doing maintenance work at the store.

Nassau County’s District Attorney pursued a charge against Walmart for reckless endangerment, which the corporation avoided by offering a $2 million settlement, $400,000 of which went to Jdimytai’s family and those injured in the stampede.

OSHA (the Occupational Safety and Health Administration) followed suit after the Nassau County DA filed a safety hazard charge against Walmart.

videos.title: Black Friday Horror - Walmart (Northridge, California) #blackfriday #walmart #horrorstories
videos.description:
Full Video: https://youtu.be/yvb88twHqNk

On November 24th, 2011, 10 minutes before the Porter Ranch Walmart opened in Los Angeles, California, a mother of two used a can of pepper spray to attack other shoppers waiting in line for the early, Black Friday door-buster sales according to the Los Angeles Times.
 
The Woman at the time was looking to get the $100 discounted price on an Xbox 360 as well as a few Xbox 360 games.
 
Once the doors opened, the woman also used the pepper spray again to gain a favorable position over other customers competing for items. A witness at the attack posted on Twitter that customers were screaming about stinging eyes.
 
Los Angeles firefighters and the LAPD responded to the attack quickly and treated 20 injured customers who suffered from extreme swelling, coughing, and redness of the face and eyes.
 
The woman would later pay for her purchases and flee the store but would later turn herself into the police.
 
She would later claim that it was self-defense as her two kids (who were with her at the time) felt traumatized when shoppers attacked them.
 
A spokeswoman for the Los Angeles District Attorney’s Office would later determine that the woman will face no felony charges.

videos.title: Black Friday Horror - Target (South Charleston, West Virginia) #blackfriday #horrorstories #target
videos.description:

On Black Friday 2011, Walter Vance, a 61-year-old pharmacist, became ill and fell to the floor as he was shopping for Christmas decorations just after midnight at a Target store in South Charleston, West Virginia.

As Vance collapsed, shoppers ignored him, continuing to shop instead of helping him. Some even stepped over him while he lay on the floor, apparently more interested in scoring the big deals and discounts. 

Some nurses who were shopping in the store came to Vance’s aid, performing CPR until paramedics arrived. However, despite their efforts, Vance later died in the hospital.

The Apple Pippin was unveiled on December 13, 1994, at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, Nevada. Three features of Apple Pippin appealed to users:

It offered low-cost access to the internet.
It brought the internet to the television.
It added convenience for consumers who wanted video games, word processing, and internet access in one device.

It was named after the Newtown Pippin, an apple cultivar, a smaller and tarter relative of the McIntosh apple (which is the namesake of the Macintosh).

Apple didn't have the resources to mass-produce hardware, so they used a business model where they licensed the technology to Bandai, who would sell the console.

Bandai projected that they'd see 14 million users within the first year of the console's release, but that didn't happen due to various delays and no licenses, which led to software developers refusing to support the console. This also led to only a few selections of video games. 

The various delays led to a March 1996 release date with outdated technology, competing against other companies who were offering affordable internet access, with the Sega Console offering that service for their "Saturn Console. 

Furthermore, the price of $599 was too expensive for consumers, and Apple was criticized for abandoning the console upon its release, leaving Bandai to try and sell it.

Pippin was discontinued in 1997 after having sold a mere 42,000 units. Ban

videos.title: “Pumper Nic” the Burger King Copycat !!?? #fastfood #pumpernic #top10
videos.description:
Video Link: https://youtu.be/kJQlYi1r37k?si=XAJHy-SZngBVkGNv

Pumper Nic was created by Alfredo Lowenstein in 1974, which would later become Argentina's first franchise.

At its peak, it operated a total of 70 restaurants and generated an annual revenue of $ 60 million.

The chain's rapid growth made it extremely difficult for its headquarters in Buenos Aires to keep a grip on the franchisees. A combination of poor management and a lack of standardization caused food quality to vary greatly between the restaurants.

Pumper Nic's signature sandwich was the Mobur, a sandwich with an egg in between. Another famous menu item was "Dos por uno" − two burgers for the price of one. French fries were called Frenys.

Pumper Nic's logo was based on Burger King's before the latter began operating in Argentina. When McDonald's and Burger King opened their first venues in the country in 1986 and 1989, respectively, Pumper Nic was forced to change its logo and have its name shortened to Pumper due to a lawsuit by Burger King.

Lowenstein handed over Pumper Nic in 1990 to his sons Diego and Paula, who had little interest in running the business. The family sold the chain in 1995 to real estate agents Goldstein and Rosenbaum

Unable to compete with larger American fast-food chains, Pumper Nic finally declared bankruptcy in early 1999.

For those curious to try them out, the Last Pumper Nic restaurant is still operating at the Moreno shopping center in Buenos Aires.

Some reports eating Nerds Cereal would produce a bright red-orange stool - an alarming, if hardly life-threatening, health condition.

videos.title: What happened to Donald Trump’s Board Game? #donaldtrump #trumpthegame #yourfired #monopolygame

Trump: The Game was launched in May by the Milton Bradley Company 1989 with the tagline, "It's not whether you win or lose, it's whether you win!" 

Jeffrey Breslow originally pitched the game to Trump, with him receiving 40 Percent of the profits while Trump received 60 Percent. 

It was reported that Breslow initially insisted that the profits would be split equally, but according to him, Trump replied, “I don’t do 50-50.” 

Donald Trump himself also appeared in a television commercial for the game.

Trump and Milton Bradley hoped the game would sell two million copies, although the game ultimately sold poorly. By August 1990, Trump acknowledged that the game may have been too complicated, with the rulebook being more than 12 pages long. 
In July 2004, the game was rereleased after the success of Trump's new reality television series, The Apprentice.

The updated version of the game implemented Trump's signature catchphrase from the series: "You're fired!"

The re-released version, priced at $25, featured somewhat simplified rules, cards with business tips for the player, and an updated box cover featuring a sterner-looking Donald Trump.

Although Breslow felt that the re-release was a superior version to the original, he said that the game did not sell well.

As of 2016, the game is considered a collector's item.

videos.title: 5 American Car Brands That Detroit Buried — And the One Pattern That Killed Every Single One
videos.description:
Five iconic American car brands are gone — and the reason they died is the same every time. Oldsmobile, Pontiac, Mercury, Saturn and DeSoto all disappeared not because buyers stopped wanting them, but because corporate decisions under financial pressure stripped away the very things that made them different. From badge-engineered platforms to mid-year cancellations, this video traces each brand's decline and the pattern hiding underneath all of them.

We open with a surprising 2026 scene: a factory near Shanghai building 1967 Mustang fastbacks and Porsche 911s — proof that American car identity still sells, decades after the companies that created it walked away. Then we follow each brand's story: Oldsmobile's badge-engineering spiral, Pontiac's identity confusion, Mercury's forty years squeezed between Ford and Lincoln, Saturn's experiment killed by the disease it was built to cure, and DeSoto's boardroom execution.

If you love automotive history, brand strategy, or just want to understand why the cars you grew up with vanished, this one is for you. Watch to the end for the pattern that still shapes Detroit's lineups today.

videos.title: 8 American Cars So Bad Detroit Wants You to Forget Them
videos.description:
Detroit has built some brilliant machines—and some cars so bad the people who made them would rather you never heard their names again. In this video, we count down eight of the worst: cars that nearly killed their brands, changed American law, and even put a company on trial for homicide. From the Pontiac Aztek to the Ford Pinto, these are the disasters that reshaped the auto industry.

You'll see how the AMC Pacer was ruined by a canceled engine, how the Cadillac Cimarron became a rebadged Cavalier, and how the Oldsmobile diesel scared Americans away from diesel for a generation. Plus, the Chevrolet Corvair that sparked Ralph Nader's crusade and the Ford Pinto that faced a reckless homicide charge. Some of these ideas were ahead of their time—the shortcuts were the problem.

Which one did your family own? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe to Forgotten Horsepower for more stories about the cars America tried to forget.

Russell Malcolm Solomon was born on September 22, 1925. His father, Clayton Solomon, was a pharmacist who ran Tower Cut-Rate Drugs inside Sacramento's Tower Theater building. Russ began working in the store at thirteen, dropped out of high school as a sophomore, and in 1941, at sixteen, began selling used jukebox records from space his father gave him at the back of the drugstore. He called it Tower Record Mart, and the theater's name became the name of his empire.

After serving as a radar technician in the Army during the Second World War, he went back to records. In the 1950s he expanded into a full sales business, buying stock on credit and working as a rack jobber who stocked other stores' shelves with vinyl. By 1960 sales had collapsed and creditors closed him down. With a 5,000 dollar loan from his father, he started again under a company called MTS, named after his son Michael. Max Factor was born Maksymilian Faktorowicz in Russian-ruled Poland, in Zduńska Wola or Łódź, sometime in the 1870s, one of ten children in a poor Jewish family. Apprenticed young to a wigmaker and a pharmacist, he made creams, rouges and wigs and later worked for theater companies tied to the tsarist court. In 1904, amid rising antisemitism, he took his wife and children to America, sold his cosmetics at the World's Fair in St. Louis, and by 1909 had opened a wig and makeup shop in Los Angeles, just as the film industry arrived.

videos.description:
In this video, we explore the DuMont Television Network, the fourth American network that gave the country Jackie Gleason's first Honeymooners sketches, Bishop Fulton Sheen and Captain Video, and the inventor behind it, Allen B. DuMont. He took money from Paramount Pictures to build it, and then watched the studio's stake keep him from adding stations, block a lifeline merger with ABC and finally help take his company away from him.

-------------------

-------------------

The first commercial Land camera arrived in 1948. Consumers no longer had to surrender film to a laboratory and wait for prints. In 1912 he ordered one hundred pairs, mailed a simple three-page flyer to non-resident Maine hunting-license holders, and offered a bold guarantee of perfect satisfaction. Ninety of those first one hundred pairs came back. The stitching had failed. The rubber had separated from the leather. Most new businesses would have collapsed under such a disaster.

Bean did the opposite. He refunded every customer in full, borrowed money, traveled to Boston, secured better rubber bottoms, improved the construction with a stronger triple stitch, and kept selling. That decision — to stand behind a defective product at the very beginning — became the foundation of one of America’s most enduring family businesses.

The lifetime guarantee that grew from those early returns became legendary. For more than a century customers could return almost anything, for almost any reason, with or without a receipt. videos.title: Unit Economics Explained: Is One More Chipotle Worth It?
videos.description:

• How to choose the unit: the thing a business multiplies when it grows, and why for Chipotle that is the restaurant

• The costs above the unit, about 9% of revenue, and why a strong unit still has to carry them

videos.title: How Blackstone Makes Money: The Fee It Never Gives Back

• Carried interest: generally up to 20% of a fund's net realized gains, usually only after investors earn a preferred return of generally 5 to 8% a year, and subject to clawback

• Perpetual capital: $523.6 billion with no fixed date to be returned, about 41% of assets under management

In this episode of How They Actually Profit, we break down the real revenue model of private hospitals: how the same square meters of floor are sold at wildly different prices through bed tiers, why the pharmacy and the laboratory quietly carry the margins (industry analyses put average medicine markups around 500 pct before negotiation, with documented studies showing margins up to 1,100 pct on some life-saving drugs), how diagnostics departments run like factories at high EBITDA margins, how the same treatment gets two different prices depending on whether cash or insurance pays, and why star doctors are revenue partners rather than employees.

This is How They Actually Profit.

videos.title: Memo: American Airlines Wants Zero Bumped Passengers
videos.description:
A full plane, one passenger too many — and American Airlines reportedly just told its agents: nobody gets bumped against their will.

When a flight is oversold and nobody volunteers, airlines can deny boarding; U.S. rules cap what an involuntarily bumped passenger is owed at 400% of the one-way fare, up to $2,150. In 2025, American accounted for more than half of all involuntary bumps by U.S. airlines. Now an internal memo dated 30 September 2026, reported by View from the Wing, says American has a "zero involuntary denied boarding mandate": the door stays open until enough volunteers are found, agents keep raising the offer, and station leaders can approve going above the old maximum. Would you take the money?

videos.title: He Mailed Pepsi $700,000 for a Fighter Jet
videos.description:
A Seattle man mailed Pepsi a check for $700,008.50 — to buy a fighter jet.

In 1996, a Pepsi Stuff TV commercial showed a Harrier jet as a prize for 7,000,000 Pepsi Points, and the rules let customers buy extra points for 10 cents each. John Leonard raised about $700,000 through acquaintances and mailed the order form, 15 original points and the check. Pepsi sent it back. In 1999 a federal judge ruled for PepsiCo: the ad was not an offer, and "an obvious joke … would not give rise to a contract." The appeals court agreed in 2000. The commercial was later changed to 700,000,000 points. Was it a joke, or a promise?

Sources:
Leonard v. PepsiCo, Inc., 88 F. Supp. 2d 116 (S.D.N.Y. 1999): https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp2/88/116/2579076/

Notes: Figures are from the court opinion (7,000,000 points; 10¢ per extra point; at least 15 original points per order; check for $700,008.50; "the cost of a Harrier Jet is roughly $23 million"). 7,000,000 × 10¢ = $700,000 is our math. The court did not say when or why the ad was changed. The closing question is ours. Generic drawings, not likenesses; no logos; not affiliated with PepsiCo. Not legal advice.

videos.title: A Truck Stop Took On the Fed Over Your Debit Card
videos.description:
A North Dakota truck stop took on the Federal Reserve — and an appeals court just sided with it.

Every debit swipe costs the store a fee that goes to the card-issuing bank. Since 2011, the Fed's Regulation II has capped that fee for big banks (over $10 billion in assets) at 21 cents plus 0.05% of the sale, plus up to 1 cent for fraud prevention. Corner Post, a truck stop and convenience store, argued the Fed let banks count costs the law doesn't allow. The case reached the Supreme Court in 2024 (on timing) and went back down. On 26 October 2026 the Eighth Circuit upheld the ruling that threw out the cap and sent the rule back to the Fed to rewrite. Stores paid about $40.5 billion in debit swipe fees in 2025. Should your swipe cost less?

videos.title: Keurig Put a Lock on Its Own Coffee Maker
videos.description:
In 2014, Keurig built a lock into its own coffee maker.

Keurig 2.0 brewers used a built-in infrared sensor that looked for invisible ink printed on each pod's foil lid. Why? The original K-Cup patents had expired in September 2012, and other companies were selling pods that fit. A pod without the ink got the message "Oops! This pack wasn't designed for this brewer." In the quarter that ended 28 March 2015, Keurig's brewer and accessory sales fell 23% from a year earlier — and CEO Brian Kelley told analysts: "Quite honestly, we were wrong." Keurig brought back its reusable My K-Cup filter. Would you have bought one?

Short sellers bet Piggly Wiggly's stock would crash. Its founder, Clarence Saunders, borrowed about $10 million and bought almost every share. videos.title: 197 Cruise Ships. Only One Flies the U.S. Flag.
videos.description:
Carnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian are all run from Miami — 197 ships between them. Only one flies the U.S. flag.

A U.S. law from the 1800s (the Passenger Vessel Services Act) lets only U.S.-flag ships carry passengers between two U.S. ports, and a U.S.-flag ship must be U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and crewed by Americans. Big cruise ships are built in Europe (Carnival's contracts are with yards in Italy and Germany), and the GAO found U.S.-flag operating costs are significantly higher. So foreign-flag ships add a foreign stop — that's why round-trip Alaska cruises from Seattle stop in Canada. The one exception, Norwegian's Pride of America in Hawaii, says its income is subject to U.S. federal and state income taxes. Carnival, incorporated in Panama, says substantially all of its income is exempt from U.S. federal income tax.

videos.description:

Why? The big number is the annuity: one payment now and 29 more over 29 years, each 5% larger than the last. The cash option is what is actually in the jackpot prize pool on draw day. Then taxes: lottery prizes have 24% federal tax withheld up front, but a prize this size is taxed at the top federal rate of 37% (2026: income over $640,600), so a winner still owes more at tax time. Before state tax, that leaves roughly $169 million — about a quarter of the headline (our math). State tax depends on the state: California, for example, doesn't tax California Lottery prizes, including Powerball.

videos.title: Why Your Concert Ticket Jumped at Checkout
videos.description:
Fans paid Ticketmaster $16.4 billion in fees from 2019 to 2024, the FTC says — about $1 of every $5 they spent on its tickets (our math: $16.4B of $82.6B).

The FTC's lawsuit (filed 18 Sep 2025 with seven states) alleges Ticketmaster advertised ticket prices without its mandatory fees, which were as high as 44% of the ticket, and added them only at the end of checkout — after internal research showed fans were less likely to buy when told the true cost up front. On 28 Sep 2026 a federal judge in California denied Live Nation and Ticketmaster's motion to dismiss, writing that "'+Fees' is vague and ambiguous". These are allegations: Live Nation and Ticketmaster deny wrongdoing and argued fans saw the full price, fees included, before paying. The case is pending.

Since 12 May 2025 the FTC's fees rule requires ticket sellers to show the total price, including mandatory fees, up front. The rule is about disclosure; it does not cap how big fees can be. The FTC also alleges Ticketmaster earned $3.7 billion in resale fees (2019–2024) while brokers used thousands of accounts (5 brokers, 6,345 accounts) to get around ticket limits.

videos.title: Your Car Loan Rate Has a Markup for the Dealer
videos.description:
Your car loan rate may include a cut for the dealer.

The lender quotes the dealer a "buy rate"; the dealer can write your contract at a higher rate and is paid part of the extra interest (CFPB). In a study of several million US car loans (2010–2014, borrowers with good credit), 78.5% were marked up; the average markup was 1.13 percentage points — 43% on top of the buy rate — and dealers received about 71 cents of every dollar of markup interest, paid up front. For a typical borrower that cost about $647 over the loan; for one in ten, over $1,655. In 2015 a federal settlement capped Honda's lender's markups at 1.25 points (from up to 2.25), and in 2018 Congress overturned the CFPB's guidance on these markups. Loans keep getting bigger: the average new-car loan was $43,610 in Q2 2026 (Experian).

videos.title: Airlines Sell More Tickets Than Seats. On Purpose.
videos.description:
Your airline sold more tickets than the plane has seats. On purpose.

Some passengers never show up, and an empty seat earns nothing, so US airlines sell extra tickets. When everyone shows up, they buy seats back: in 2018 about 340,000 passengers on big US airlines gave up their seat for compensation, while about 10,000 were bumped involuntarily (GAO). Involuntary bumping is now rare (0.25 per 10,000 passengers in Q4 2024, DOT). US rules require up to 400% of the one-way fare, capped at $2,150, for involuntary bumping with long delays — and if the airline offers a voucher instead, it must tell you the cash amount and that you can take cash. In April 2017 Delta let supervisors offer volunteers up to $9,950 (AP). "It's an auction / a price tag" is our take.

videos.title: How Food Delivery Apps Make Money From Your $40 Order?
videos.description:

This is how food delivery apps make money, told through one fictional $40 order.

Ethan orders a $30 meal. By checkout it becomes $40: a $3 delivery fee, a $2 service fee, $2 in sales tax, and a $3 tip for the driver. The platform also takes a 25% commission from the restaurant, so the restaurant receives $22.50 from the $30 food price. After $11 in ingredients and packaging and $8 in kitchen labour and operating expenses, only $3.50 is left before additional expenses. The driver receives $5 in base pay plus the $3 tip, $8 in total, and after $2 in vehicle expenses, $6 is left before taxes and time.

The platform collects $5 in customer fees plus $7.50 in commission, $12.50 in total. After the driver's $5 base pay, $1.20 in processing costs, and $4.50 in allocated operating costs, only $1.80 remains before additional expenses. And on a rainy evening, one extra $2 incentive to get the delivery accepted turns that $1.80 into a 20-cent loss. Same customer, same dinner, same price — a completely different financial outcome.

videos.title: $8 Billion Debt: Why 82% Popcorn Margins Fail to Save Movie Theaters
videos.description:
In 2025, theaters kept 82 cents of every dollar spent at the snack counter, but only 49 cents of every ticket.
We calculate the actual gross profit per 100,000 guests to see where the money sits and why it isn't enough.

Going to the movies feels like a simple transaction: you pay for a ticket, you watch a film. But behind the screen is a financial architecture built on split revenues, concession margins, and massive liabilities. Looking at the 2025 annual reports filed with the SEC by giants like AMC and Cinemark, the real business model of the multiplex emerges.

The data reveals two entirely different pockets. One pocket is the box office, split almost evenly with the studios who own the films. The other is the lobby, where the theater owns the food, the drinks, and the advertising network. Yet, despite generating billions from high-margin snacks and premium format fees, theater chains carry billions in corporate borrowings and operational leases. We break down the exact costs of film exhibition versus concession supplies to see what a buyer actually gets when acquiring a cinema.

Disclaimer: This video is an educational analysis based on public financial reports and SEC filings. It does not contain investment advice or financial recommendations.

videos.title: The Eiffel Tower Was Sold... Twice 🗼  #victorlustig #eiffeltower #paris1925 #conman #historyfacts
videos.description:
In 1925, Victor Lustig "sold" the Eiffel Tower for scrap metal. 🗼

He invited scrap-metal dealers to the Hôtel de Crillon in Paris and posed as a senior government official from the Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs. The city, he claimed, could no longer afford to maintain the tower, and it would be sold for scrap. He had already picked his buyer: André Poisson, a man eager to join Paris's business elite. Poisson paid, and was then too embarrassed to go to the police. So Lustig returned and tried again with a new group of dealers. This time the police were informed, and Lustig fled to America.

"Sold twice" is the popular telling. Accounts differ on whether the second sale was completed, so we show the second attempt as it is usually told. The tower itself was never for sale.

All scenes are drawn illustrations, not footage.

Would you have fallen for it? 👇

videos.title: The Sahara Was Green 6,000 Years Ago 🌿 #shorts
videos.description:
The Sahara was GREEN 6,000 years ago. Lakes. Grasslands. Even hippos. 🦛🌿

So why is it a desert now? 👇 Earth wobbles like a spinning top. Combined with its orbit, that shifts how much summer sun the north gets, in a cycle of about 21,000 years.

☀️ Stronger summers pulled Africa's monsoon rains over the Sahara
🌧️ Then the cycle turned and the rains drifted south
🍂 Plants died, bare ground reflected more sunlight, and the drying sped up. In some places, within a few centuries.

Rock paintings in Egypt's "Cave of Swimmers" show what look like people swimming, in one of the driest places on Earth.

Will it turn green again? Tell me 🌿 or 🏜️ in the comments.

Follow for more places where Earth breaks the rules 🌍

📚 Sources: Shanahan et al. 2015 (Nature Geoscience), deMenocal et al. 2000, University of Helsinki 2023, Eos, Wadi Sura project (University of Cologne)

videos.title: The Sun Doesn't Set Here for 127 Days ☀️ #shorts #midnightsun #geography #alaska #iceland #facts
videos.description:
In some countries, the sun doesn't set for months. Not hours. Months. ☀️

Why? Earth is tilted about 23.4°. In summer the far north leans toward the sun, so even as the planet spins, it never turns into night.

🇮🇸 Iceland: only Grímsey, the one island on the Arctic Circle, a few days around June 21
🇸🇪 Sweden (Abisko): about 8 weeks
🇷🇺 Russia (Murmansk): 62 days
🇫🇮 Finland (Utsjoki): 70+ days
🇺🇸 Alaska (Utqiagvik): 84 days
🇳🇴 Norway (Svalbard / Longyearbyen): about 127 days
…and in winter, the same tilt hides the sun in Svalbard for about 82 days.

Dates vary by a day or two depending on the source and how sunrise is defined.

📚 Sources: Visit Svalbard / Yr (Norwegian Meteorological Institute); Visit Sweden citing SMHI; Explore Utsjoki; Akureyri town (Grímsey); Murmansk regional government; NOAA and news reports on Utqiagvik (2026).

Canada and Greenland have it too. Which one should be next? 👇

videos.title: Japan Sent Thousands of Bombs Across the Pacific to Attack America
videos.description:
In 1945, a minister's wife in Oregon pulled her car off the road for a picnic. Minutes later, she was dead, killed by a weapon that had been launched from Japan, roughly 6,000 miles away. It had made the trip using no engine, no pilot, and no fuel. It was made of paper, glue, and hydrogen.

Between late 1944 and spring 1945, Japan launched about nine thousand of these balloons at North America. They reached from Alaska to Mexico, and even Michigan. And for months, almost nobody in America heard a word about it.

That is the strangest part of this story. The weapon worked. The secrecy worked too. And that secrecy ended up wrecking the whole program.

A note on the title: the weapon was a balloon carrying a small bomb, not a bomber or a missile, and the balloons landed in Canada and Mexico as well as the United States. Figures such as the number launched and the number that arrived are estimates.

In this video, we tell the story of the Fu-Go, the Japanese "wind-ship weapon."

videos.title: 16 American Bombers Took Off to Attack Japan — But None Could Return Home - WW2
videos.description:
Sixteen bombers took off from the deck of an aircraft carrier in April of 1942, and not one of them was ever supposed to land on it again. They were Army planes, far too big and heavy for a Navy flight deck. Nobody had ever launched aircraft like this from a carrier in combat. And the target was Tokyo.

The crews were told to bomb Japan, then keep flying west to friendly airfields in China, about two thousand miles away. The raid itself destroyed surprisingly little. By strict military math, it was a failure. Yet it changed the direction of the war in the Pacific.

A note on the title: none of the 16 planes ever came home, but most of the 80 airmen did. We explain what happened to the men, and to the Chinese civilians who helped them.

So how does a mission fail at nearly everything and still matter this much?

📚 WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
• Why America needed a symbolic strike on Japan after Pearl Harbor
• How a Navy officer's idea led to launching Army bombers from a carrier
• How the B-25 was modified, from extra fuel tanks to broomstick "guns"
• Why the fleet had to launch about 650 miles from Japan, far earlier than planned
• Why the raid did so little physical damage
• Why almost every crew had to bail out over China
• How Captain Edward York's crew ended up in the Soviet Union
• How Chinese villagers helped the airmen, and the heavy price civilians paid in Japan's retaliation
• What happened to the raiders, including Jacob DeShazer
• How the raid influenced Japan's decisions

videos.title: The submarine that disappeared in the Atlantic… and its crew never returned
videos.description:
On the morning of November 15, 2017, an Argentine submarine sent a routine report to its headquarters. Seawater had leaked into the battery system. There had been a short circuit and some smoke. The crew had isolated the damaged section and was carrying on. Nothing in that message sounded like the opening of a national tragedy.

It was the last message anyone would ever receive from the A.R.A. San Juan. There were 44 people on board.

Within days, ships and aircraft from about eighteen countries were searching the South Atlantic. The submarine was found a year and a day after that final message, roughly 900 meters underwater. So how does a steel submarine vanish in an age of satellites and sonar? And why did the answer take so long to surface?

In this video, we tell the story of the A.R.A. San Juan, from its last message to the discovery of the wreck.


📚 WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
• What a diesel-electric submarine is and why its batteries are both its heart and its greatest danger
• What the crew reported in the final message
• Why hopes of a rescue, such as satellite calls and tapping sounds, did not hold up
• How an international monitoring network recorded a sound consistent with an explosion
• How Ocean Infinity used autonomous underwater vehicles to find the wreck
• What the Navy and later analysts concluded about the implosion
• Why the refit, the maintenance, and the Navy's response are still debated
• Why the full chain of events that led to the disaster is still disputed

videos.title: 500 Men Escaped From a Nazi Prison Camp — Then Hitler Ordered a Manhunt
videos.description:
Picture a barracks built for a few hundred people, holding around 570. No heat, almost no food, and a bucket of water as the closest thing to plumbing. Now picture those men, in the middle of a freezing Austrian winter, deciding to run, past machine guns, searchlights, and an electrified fence.

On the night of February 2, 1945, about 419 Soviet prisoners got out of Block 20 at Mauthausen. Then the real nightmare began: the people hunting them were not just the SS. They were farmers, teenagers, and neighbors.

A note on the title: the figure of 500 is a round number. About 570 men were held in Block 20, and roughly 419 made it outside the wire. And while the manhunt followed orders from regional Nazi leadership and the SS, no order signed by Hitler himself has been established. We explain exactly what the evidence shows.

This is the story of the Mühlviertel hare hunt, and of the few men who survived it.

📚 WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
• What Block 20 was and why Soviet prisoners of war were held there

videos.title: The German Sniper Who Became a Legend on the Eastern Front
videos.description:
The most famous German sniper of the Eastern Front may never have existed. Legend says he was a Major König, sent to Stalingrad to hunt down the Soviet hero Vasily Zaitsev. Historians have searched for him for decades and found almost nothing.

The real record points elsewhere: to a quiet Austrian farm boy named Matthäus Hetzenauer, who had no famous duel and was credited with 345 kills in about six months of front-line shooting.

So why does the world remember the man who probably never existed, while the man who actually did it is barely known?

In this video, we separate the legend from the record, and look at how a war turned snipers into celebrities.

• Why Hetzenauer was Austrian, not German, and what that meant in 1944

• Why patience mattered more than the rifle

videos.title: He Charged Into Enemy Fire to Save His Entire Unit
videos.description:
On May 5, 1945, an American infantry battalion ran into one of the worst places on Earth: a four-hundred-foot cliff on Okinawa, packed with Japanese machine guns, mortars, and hidden tunnels. Hundreds of soldiers climbed it. Most of them came back down very fast.

One man stayed. He was surrounded by wounded soldiers, and he did not own a weapon. He had a bag of medical supplies and a length of rope.

How did the man his own unit called a coward end up saving dozens of lives? This is the story of Desmond Doss, the first conscientious objector to receive the Medal of Honor, and the battle for Hacksaw Ridge.


📚 WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
• Why Doss refused to carry a weapon, and how he preferred to be called a "conscientious cooperator"
