videos.title: Slavic Gods: The Real Myths vs Modern Forgeries

videos.title: Why Did Egyptians Worship Cats? | Bastet, Ra's Great Cat and 180,000 Mummies in Liverpool
videos.description:
Ancient Egyptians killed a Roman for killing a cat. Then Liverpool sold their cats as fertiliser.

In the Book of the Dead (spell 17), the sun god Ra takes the form of the Great Cat of Heliopolis and cuts off the head of the chaos serpent Apophis beside the sacred persea tree. The goddess Bastet, first shown as a lioness, came to be shown as a cat. Herodotus (Histories 2.66) says that when a household cat died, everyone in the house shaved their eyebrows. Diodorus Siculus (1.83) saw a Roman who had killed a cat by accident lynched by a mob in Egypt, although officials sent by the king tried to save him.

On 10 February 1890, an estimated 180,000 mummified cats, about 19.5 tons, taken from Istabl Antar near Beni Hasan, were auctioned in Liverpool to be ground into fertiliser, at a few pounds a ton; the auctioneer is reported to have used a cat's head as his hammer. A few of the heads were given to the museum and are still in National Museums Liverpool.

videos.title: Why Did Susanoo Get a Serpent Drunk? | Yamata no Orochi and the Sword Kusanagi (Part 2)
videos.description:
A god got an eight-headed serpent drunk and found a sword in its tail.

In the Kojiki (712), the storm god Susanoo is punished for the rampage that made his sister, the sun goddess Amaterasu, hide in the Heavenly Rock Cave: the gods fine him, cut off his beard, pull out his nails and expel him from heaven. He comes down by the river Hi in Izumo, sees chopsticks floating downstream and finds an old couple, Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi, weeping beside their daughter Kushinadahime. The eight-forked serpent of Koshi, Yamata no Orochi, has eaten one of their eight daughters every year. Its eyes are red as winter cherries, moss and cypress trees grow on its body, and it stretches across eight valleys and eight hills. Susanoo turns the girl into a comb and puts it in his hair, has the couple brew eight-times-refined sake and builds a fence with eight gates, with a vat of sake at each. The serpent dips a head into every vat, drinks, and falls asleep. Susanoo cuts it to pieces and the river Hi runs red. When he cuts the middle tail, the edge of his sword breaks: inside is a great sword, which he presents to Amaterasu. It is later called Kusanagi, the grass-cutter, after the prince Yamato Takeru mowed down a burning grass plain with it.

Kusanagi is one of the three imperial regalia of Japan and is kept at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya. It is never put on show: at the accession ceremony of 1 May 2019, the sword and the jewel were handed to the new emperor in covered boxes.

videos.title: Why Do People Light Lamps for Diwali? | Rama, Ravana and the Ten Heads
videos.description:
A king with ten heads made himself god-proof, then lost to a man and some monkeys.

In Valmiki's Ramayana, Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka, wins a boon from the creator god Brahma: no god, demon or other powerful being can kill him. He does not ask for protection from humans, whom he dismisses as straw (Uttara Kanda 7.10). He abducts Sita, wife of Prince Rama. Hanuman, son of the wind god, leaps the ocean and finds her (Sundara Kanda). The monkey engineer Nala builds a bridge across the sea in five days (Yuddha Kanda 6.22). In battle, every head Rama cuts off grows back (6.107), until he fires Brahma's own weapon through Ravana's heart (6.108). Rama, Vishnu born as a man, returns home to Ayodhya, and in popular tradition the city lights rows of lamps to welcome him, one of the stories behind Diwali.

Ayodhya's Deepotsav still lights lamps along the Sarayu every Diwali and keeps breaking its own Guinness World Record: 2,512,585 oil lamps in 2024 and 2,617,215 on 19 October 2025, all lit within 25 minutes.

videos.title: How Did Thor Catch the World Serpent? | Jormungandr, Hymir and the Altuna Stone (Part 2)
videos.description:
Thor went fishing for the serpent that circles the world. The bait was an ox's head.

In Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning 48, written in Iceland around 1220), Thor takes his revenge for what happened at Utgard, where the giant Utgarda-Loki had made him lift a cat that was really the Midgard Serpent. Disguised as a young lad, Thor spends the night at the house of the giant Hymir and asks to go fishing with him. Hymir tells him to find his own bait, so Thor tears the head off Hymir's biggest ox, Himinhrjodr. He rows far past the banks where Hymir fishes for flatfish, out where the giant fears the serpent. The serpent bites the ox head and the hook sticks in its mouth; it pulls so hard that Thor's fists hit the gunwale, and Thor, taking on his divine strength, braces so hard that both his feet go through the boat and he stands on the sea floor. Thor glares at the serpent, the serpent stares back and blows poison, and as Thor raises his hammer, the terrified Hymir cuts the line with his bait knife. Some say Thor knocked its head off on the seabed; Snorri writes that he thinks the serpent is still alive in the sea around the world. Thor punches Hymir overboard and wades ashore. In the older poem Hymiskvida, the giant catches two whales at once and Thor strikes the serpent's head before it sinks.

They meet again at Ragnarok: Thor kills the serpent, walks nine steps away and falls dead from its venom (Gylfaginning 51; Voluspa).

videos.title: Why Is a Demon Burned Before Diwali? | Narakasura, Krishna and Satyabhama
videos.description:
A demon could only be killed by his own mother, so he felt safe. He didn't recognise her.

In the Bhagavata Purana (10.59), Krishna, riding the eagle Garuda with his wife Satyabhama, attacks the fortress of Narakasura, the son of the Earth goddess Bhudevi, who had stolen the earrings of Aditi and held sixteen thousand women captive. Krishna kills him and the women are released. In later regional and devotional tellings, Narakasura could only be killed by his own mother; Krishna falls in the battle, Satyabhama, who is Bhudevi reborn, takes up his bow and kills the demon, and his last wish is that the day of his death be celebrated with lights. That day is Naraka Chaturdashi, also called Choti Diwali, the day before the main day of Diwali.

In Goa, neighbourhoods build Narakasura effigies twenty feet tall or more, filled with grass and firecrackers, parade them through the night and burn them before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi.

videos.title: Why Did Maui Lasso the Sun? | Haleakalā, the House of the Sun, in Hawaiian Mythology
videos.description:
The demigod from Moana lassoed the sun and beat it up, all because of his mother's laundry.

In the Hawaiian tradition recorded by W. D. Westervelt in Legends of Ma-ui (1910, chapter IV) and summarised by Martha Beckwith in Hawaiian Mythology (1940), the sun crossed the sky so quickly that Hina, Maui's mother, could never dry her kapa, her bark cloth. Maui climbed Haleakalā, where his grandmother cooked bananas for the sun each morning. He stole them until she found him, and then she helped him. The sun had sixteen legs, its rays; Maui snared them with sixteen ropes, the last one given by his grandmother, and beat the sun with a stone club until it begged for its life. The bargain: it would travel slowly for half the year, which is why summer days are long.

Haleakalā means house of the sun. Since 2017, Haleakalā National Park has required a reservation to drive in between 3 and 7 a.m. for the sunrise, and the National Park Service says it often sells out within fifteen minutes.

videos.title: How Did Thor Lose to an Old Woman? | Utgarda-Loki's Tricks in Norse Mythology
videos.description:
Thor lost to a cat, an old woman and a drinking horn. The giants were terrified.

In Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (Gylfaginning, chapters 44 to 47, written in Iceland around 1220), Thor and Loki visit the hall of the giant Utgarda-Loki and are challenged to contests. Loki loses an eating contest to Logi, who eats the meat, the bones and the trough. Thor fails to empty a drinking horn, lifts only one paw of a grey cat, and is forced down to one knee by an old woman called Elli. The next morning the giant reveals that it was all illusion: Logi was wildfire, the cat was the Midgard Serpent, the horn's far end was in the sea (Snorri says that is how the ebb tide began), and Elli was old age, which no one can beat. The giants had been terrified the whole time.

videos.title: Why Did Horus Behead His Mother Isis? | The Hippo Contest and Tutankhamun's Harpoon Statues
videos.description:
Two gods turned into hippos to win a throne, and one beheaded his own mother.

In The Contendings of Horus and Seth (Papyrus Chester Beatty I, about 1160 BC, Chester Beatty Library, Dublin; translated by Alan Gardiner in 1931), Horus and his uncle Seth turn into hippopotamuses and dive: whoever comes up before three months have passed loses the throne. Isis makes a harpoon from one deben of copper and throws it into the water. It hits Horus, and she releases it. Her second throw hits Seth, who pleads with her as his sister, and she releases him as well. Enraged, Horus comes out, cuts off his mother's head and carries it up the mountain, and her headless body becomes a statue of flint. In another papyrus (Sallier IV), Thoth gives her a new head: a cow's.

Howard Carter found the first step of Tutankhamun's tomb on 4 November 1922. Among its treasures were two gilded wooden statuettes (Carter 275c and 275e) of the king standing on a papyrus skiff with a harpoon raised, as Horus hunting Seth. The hippo is never shown, because Seth was thought too dangerous to depict. The statuettes are now part of Tutankhamun's collection at the Grand Egyptian Museum, Giza.

The full trial of Horus and Seth, which lasted eighty years, is told in the MythologyNow app.

videos.title: Why Does Sisyphus Push a Boulder Forever? | The King Who Chained Up Death
videos.description:
A king chained up Death, so nobody on Earth could die.

Sisyphus, king of Corinth, tells the river god Asopus that Zeus has carried off his daughter Aegina, and in return Asopus gives Corinth a spring (Pausanias 2.5.1). Zeus sends Death, Thanatos, for him, and Sisyphus puts Death in chains, so for a while no one can die. When Death is released and Sisyphus dies, he has already told his wife not to send the customary offerings; in the underworld he persuades its rulers to let him go back and punish her, and he lives on until old age. In the oldest full account, by Pherecydes (preserved in the scholia on Iliad 6.153), Hades then makes him roll a rock so that he cannot run away again. Theognis says he talked Persephone round with wily words, and Homer's Odyssey (11.593-600) describes the stone that always rolls back down just before the top.

An Athenian black-figure amphora of about 530 BC, attributed to the Swing Painter and now in the Staatliche Antikensammlungen in Munich, shows Persephone watching Sisyphus push the stone.

videos.title: What Happened When Izanagi Looked at Izanami? | Yomi, the Japanese Land of the Dead
videos.description:
He went to bring his wife back from the dead, and she swore to kill a thousand people a day.

In the Kojiki, compiled in 712 and the oldest surviving Japanese chronicle, the creator god Izanagi goes down to Yomi, the land of the dead, to bring back his wife Izanami. She has already eaten at the hearth of Yomi, but she agrees to ask the gods of Yomi to let her return, as long as he does not look at her. Impatient, he breaks off the end tooth of his comb, lights it, and sees her body rotting, with eight thunder gods living in it. Shamed, she sends the hags of Yomi after him, then the eight thunder gods with an army of fifteen hundred. He escapes by throwing his headdress (it turns into grapes), his comb (bamboo shoots) and three peaches, and blocks the pass, Yomotsu Hirasaka, with a rock it would take a thousand men to move. Across it, Izanami vows to strangle a thousand people a day, and Izanagi answers that he will build fifteen hundred birthing huts a day. The Kojiki says that is why each day a thousand die and fifteen hundred are born.

In Higashiizumo, Matsue, in Shimane Prefecture, a hillside is marked as Yomotsu Hirasaka, with stone pillars, a sacred shimenawa rope, large rocks and peach trees. Since 2017 it has had a postbox for letters to the dead, which a Shinto priest burns once a year.

videos.title: Where Do Humans Come From in Aztec Myth? | Quetzalcoatl and the Stolen Bones of Mictlan
videos.description:
The Aztecs said you're made of stolen bones, and the god who stole them dropped them.

In the Leyenda de los Soles (1558), Quetzalcoatl goes down to Mictlan to take the precious bones from Mictlantecuhtli, the lord of the dead. Mictlantecuhtli sets him a test: blow a conch shell trumpet that has no holes. Quetzalcoatl calls worms to drill the holes and bees to make it sound. Then the lord of the dead has a pit dug for him; Quetzalcoatl falls in, is startled by quail, drops dead for a moment, and the bones are scattered and broken. The goddess Cihuacoatl grinds them, and Quetzalcoatl and the other gods bleed on them to make the new humans. In the version told by the friar Gerónimo de Mendieta, the bone breaks into bigger and smaller pieces, and that is why people come in different sizes.

In August 1994, archaeologists excavating the House of the Eagles at the Templo Mayor in Mexico City found two life-size clay statues of Mictlantecuhtli, about 1.74 m tall, with the liver hanging below the ribs. They had been crushed into hundreds of pieces and were glued back together; they are now in the Museo del Templo Mayor (López Luján and Mercado, Estudios de Cultura Náhuatl 26, 1996).

videos.title: Why Do We Carve Jack-o'-Lanterns? | Stingy Jack, the Devil and Ireland's Turnip Lanterns
videos.description:
The first jack-o'-lantern was a turnip, carried by a man too wicked for heaven and too clever for hell.

In the Irish folk legend of Stingy Jack, told in many versions since the 18th and 19th centuries, Jack invites the Devil for a drink and won't pay. He persuades the Devil to turn himself into a coin to settle the bill, then pockets it beside a silver cross so the Devil can't change back. Another time he tricks the Devil into climbing an apple tree and carves a cross into the bark so he can't come down. Each time Jack lets him go in exchange for a promise never to claim his soul. When Jack dies, heaven turns him away, and the Devil, bound by his promise, won't take him either. He sends Jack into the dark with a single ember from hell, which Jack places inside a hollowed-out turnip. Jack of the lantern has wandered ever since.

At Samhain, people in Ireland carved faces into turnips long before pumpkins; Irish emigrants later took the custom to America, where pumpkins were bigger and easier to carve. The National Museum of Ireland, Country Life, in County Mayo, displays a plaster cast of a turnip lantern carved in Donegal around 1900 and donated in 1943.

videos.title: How Did Savitri Outwit the God of Death? | Yama, Satyavan and the Mahabharata
videos.description:
A woman followed Death himself, and talked him into giving her husband back.

In the Mahabharata (Book III, the Vana Parva), Princess Savitri chooses to marry Satyavan, the son of an exiled blind king, although the sage Narada warns that he will die within a year. On the fated day Satyavan collapses in the forest with his head in her lap, and Yama, the god of death, draws out his soul, the size of a thumb, with his noose. Savitri follows Yama, and her wise words move him to grant her boons, anything except her husband's life: her father-in-law's sight, his lost kingdom, a hundred sons for her own father, and finally a hundred sons for herself, by Satyavan. Bound by his word, Yama returns Satyavan's life.

Vat Savitri (also called Vat Purnima) is still observed in the month of Jyeshtha. Married women across northern and western India fast for her and wind thread around a banyan tree, the tree under which Savitri won her husband back.

videos.title: How Did a Snake Steal Eternal Life From Gilgamesh? | The Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI
videos.description:
The first hero in history found the plant of eternal life, and lost it to a snake while he took a bath.

In the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh (Tablets X and XI), the death of his friend Enkidu leaves Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, terrified of dying. He crosses the waters of death with the boatman Urshanabi, using three hundred punting poles so his hands never touch the water, and reaches Utnapishtim, the survivor of the Flood, whom the gods made immortal. Utnapishtim challenges him to stay awake for six days and seven nights; Gilgamesh falls asleep at once, and Utnapishtim's wife bakes a loaf for each day he sleeps. As a parting gift Gilgamesh learns of a thorny plant at the bottom of the Apsu, the deep waters, whose name is "The Old Man Grows Young". He ties stones to his feet, dives and takes it. On the way home he bathes in a pool; a snake smells the fragrance of the plant, carries it off, and sheds its skin as it goes. Gilgamesh sits down and weeps.

Tablet XI, the Flood Tablet (K.3375, Nineveh, 7th century BC), is in the British Museum. When George Smith deciphered its Flood story in 1872, he reportedly became so excited that he began to undress.

videos.title: Why Did the Sun Goddess Hide in a Cave? | Amaterasu, Susanoo and the Hidden Mirror of Ise
videos.description:
The sun goddess locked herself in a cave, and the whole world went dark.

In the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720), the storm god Susanoo runs wild in heaven: he wrecks his sister Amaterasu's rice fields and throws a flayed horse through the roof of her sacred weaving hall. The sun goddess hides in the Heavenly Rock Cave, Ama-no-Iwato, and the world falls into darkness. The eight million gods gather outside. They hang a mirror and jewels on a sakaki tree, set the long-crying roosters crowing, and the goddess Ame-no-Uzume dances on an upturned tub until the gods roar with laughter. Amaterasu peeks out to see what the noise is, is told there is a goddess even more radiant than her, and sees her own reflection in the mirror. The strong god Ame-no-Tajikarao pulls her out, and a sacred rope is stretched across the cave so she cannot hide again.

That mirror, Yata no Kagami, one of the three Imperial Regalia of Japan, is said to be enshrined at the Ise Grand Shrine, wrapped and hidden. It has never been shown to the public. The shrine is rebuilt every 20 years; the next rebuilding is due in 2033.

videos.title: How Did Isis Steal Ra's Secret Name? | The Snake, the Spit and a Spell in Turin
videos.description:
A goddess poisoned the sun god with his own spit, and cured him only for his secret name.

In the Egyptian text known as Isis and the Name of Ra, from the Ramesside period (around 1200 BC), the sun god Ra has grown old and drools as he travels across the sky. Isis kneads his spittle with earth into a snake and leaves it on his path. The snake bites him and his cry reaches the heavens. Isis offers to cure him only if he tells her his true, hidden name. Ra first recites his other names (Khepri in the morning, Ra at noon, Atum in the evening), but the poison does not leave him. At last he agrees, on condition that she pass the name only to her son Horus, and the name passes from his heart into hers.

The story was used as a healing spell against poison, recited for people stung by scorpions or bitten by snakes. It survives in Papyrus Turin 1993 and on ostraca from Deir el-Medina, the village of the royal tomb builders. The secret name is never written in it.

videos.title: Why Did Thor Wear a Wedding Dress? | Thrym, Loki and the Stolen Hammer
videos.description:
The strongest god in Norse myth got his hammer back in a wedding dress.

In the Thrymskvida, a poem of the Poetic Edda, Thor wakes to find his hammer Mjolnir gone. Loki borrows Freyja's falcon cloak and learns that the giant Thrym has buried it eight leagues underground, and will return it only if Freyja becomes his bride. Freyja snorts with such rage that her necklace, Brisingamen, bursts. Heimdall suggests the solution: dress Thor as the bride. Thor goes veiled, with Loki as his bridesmaid. At the feast the bride eats an ox, eight salmon and all the delicacies meant for the women, and drinks three casks of mead; Loki explains that Freyja had not eaten for eight nights out of longing. Thrym orders the hammer brought in to hallow the bride and laid in her lap, and Thor takes it back.

The Kobelev amulet, found by a metal detectorist on Lolland, Denmark, and published in 2014, is a 10th-century Thor's hammer pendant. Of about 1,000 known hammer amulets, it is the only one with a runic inscription: "Hmar x is", this is a hammer.

videos.title: Why Did the Aztecs Need a Dog to Reach the Afterlife? | Mictlan, Xolotl and the River of the Dead
videos.description:
To reach the land of the dead, the Aztecs believed you needed a dog.

In the Florentine Codex, compiled by Bernardino de Sahagún with Nahua scholars in the 16th century, the dead travel for four years to Mictlan, the land of the dead, through nine levels: two mountains that clash together, a serpent and a lizard guarding the road, eight deserts and eight hills, and a wind of obsidian knives. At the end lies a river that can only be crossed on the back of a dog. In some accounts a white dog refuses, saying it has just washed itself, and a black dog refuses because it has just got dirty; only a yellow or tawny dog will carry the dead across. That is why a small dog was sent with the dead, with a loose cotton thread tied around its neck. The god Xolotl, the dog-headed guide of souls, gives his name to the Xoloitzcuintle, the hairless dog of Mexico.

In western Mexico, in the shaft tombs of Colima (around 300 BC to AD 300), people placed clay dogs beside the dead some two thousand years ago.

videos.title: Why Is the Owl Called Flower-Face in Welsh? | Blodeuwedd and the Mabinogi
videos.description:
A wizard made a woman out of flowers, and when she betrayed him, he turned her into an owl.

In the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi (Math fab Mathonwy), Arianrhod curses her son Lleu Llaw Gyffes never to have a wife of any race now on earth. The magicians Math and Gwydion conjure him one from the flowers of the oak, the broom and the meadowsweet, and name her Blodeuwedd, "flower-face". While Lleu is away, she falls in love with Gronw Pebyr, lord of Penllyn, and they plot his death. Lleu can only be killed in one way: by a spear worked on for a year, only during Sunday Mass, while he stands with one foot on a goat and the other on the edge of a bath, under a thatched roof by a riverbank. Blodeuwedd persuades him to show her the pose, and Gronw throws. Lleu turns into an eagle and flies off wounded; Gwydion finds him by following a sow, and heals him. Gwydion turns Blodeuwedd into an owl, never to show her face in daylight and hated by all other birds.

The Mabinogi says the owl is still called Blodeuwedd, and in Welsh the word still means owl.

videos.title: What If You Lived Forever but Kept Aging? | Tithonus, Eos and Sappho's Lost Poem
videos.description:
She asked the gods to let him live forever, and forgot to ask that he stay young.

In the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite, Eos, the goddess of dawn, falls in love with Tithonus, a prince of Troy, and asks Zeus to make him immortal. Zeus grants it, but she never asks for eternal youth. While he is young she lives with him by the streams of Ocean at the ends of the earth; when grey hair comes, she keeps away from his bed, and when he can no longer move his limbs, she shuts him in a room behind shining doors, where his voice flows on endlessly. In the Iliad, Dawn rises every morning from the bed of Tithonus. Later Greek tradition said he shrank into a cicada, singing at every dawn.

In 2004, scholars in Cologne published a papyrus recovered from Egyptian mummy cartonnage and copied in the early 3rd century BC: the oldest manuscript of Sappho ever found. Together with a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, it completed her poem about Tithonus and old age: being human, it is not possible to escape growing old.

videos.title: Why Did Narcissus Fall in Love With Himself? | Echo, Nemesis and a Poisonous Flower
videos.description:
The first narcissist died staring at a puddle.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book III), the seer Tiresias tells the nymph Liriope that her son Narcissus will live a long life "if he never knows himself". Narcissus grows up so beautiful that young men and nymphs fall for him, and he scorns them all. The nymph Echo, cursed by Juno to repeat only the last words of others, pines away for him until only her voice remains. One of the youths he rejected prays that Narcissus may love in the same way and never possess what he loves, and Nemesis, the goddess of retribution, hears the prayer. Leaning over a clear pool to drink, Narcissus falls in love with his own reflection, realises too late that it is himself, and wastes away. In place of his body the nymphs find a flower with a yellow centre and white petals: the narcissus, a plant that is poisonous in every part. Pliny the Elder disagreed about the name: he said it came from narke, "numbness", not from the boy of the fable.

In 2019, archaeologists in Pompeii (Regio V) uncovered a well-preserved fresco of Narcissus gazing at his reflection in the entrance hall of a house. The site's director called the myth a very common subject in the ancient city.

videos.title: How Did a One-Day-Old Baby Steal Apollo's Cows? | Hermes, the First Lyre and a Louvre Vase
videos.description:
A baby one day old stole fifty cows and made them walk backwards.

In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes (around the 6th century BC), Hermes is born at dawn in a cave on Mount Cyllene, son of Zeus and the nymph Maia. By noon he finds a tortoise and makes the first lyre from its shell. That evening he steals fifty cows from the herd of his brother Apollo, drives them backwards so their hoofprints point the wrong way, and binds sandals of tamarisk and myrtle twigs to his own feet to hide his tracks. Back home by dawn, he slips through the keyhole like autumn mist and lies in his cradle. When Apollo comes for his cattle, Hermes swears he is a newborn who knows nothing about cows. Zeus laughs at the lie. Apollo hears the lyre, falls in love with it, and trades the herd for it, calling Hermes the prince of thieves.

The Caeretan hydria in the Louvre (E 702, around 530 to 520 BC) shows the moment: baby Hermes in his cradle inside the cave, Apollo arriving, and the stolen cows hidden by the entrance.

videos.title: How Did Loki Lose a Bet and Keep His Head? | Brokkr, Mjolnir and the Snaptun Stone
videos.description:
Loki bet his head, lost the bet, and still kept it.

In Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda (Skaldskaparmal), Loki bets his head that the dwarf Brokkr's brother cannot forge treasures as fine as the ones the sons of Ivaldi made for the gods: Sif's golden hair, the ship Skidbladnir and Odin's spear Gungnir. While Brokkr works the bellows, a fly stings his hand, his neck and his eyelids. Snorri never says who the fly is, but almost every reader blames Loki. From the forge come the golden boar Gullinbursti, the ring Draupnir and Thor's hammer Mjolnir, whose handle came out short because Brokkr let go of the bellows for a moment. Odin, Thor and Freyr judge the hammer the best treasure of all, so Brokkr wins. When he comes for Loki's head, Loki says the head is his but the neck is not, and Brokkr cannot take one without the other. So he sews Loki's lips shut with his brother's awl.

The Snaptun Stone, found on a beach near Snaptun, Denmark, in 1950, is a soapstone forge stone carved around the year 1000 with a moustached face and scarred lips, usually identified as Loki. The bellows' nozzle went through its hole, and the stone shielded the bellows from the fire. It is now in Moesgaard Museum, near Aarhus.

videos.title: Why Was Osiris Cut Into 14 Pieces? | Set, Isis and the First Mummy in Egyptian Mythology
videos.description:
A king was cut into fourteen pieces by his own brother, put back together by his wife, and became the first mummy.

In Plutarch's On Isis and Osiris, the fullest version of the myth, Set secretly measures his brother Osiris and has a beautiful chest made to his exact size. At a banquet he promises it to whoever fits inside. Osiris lies down, Set and his accomplices slam the lid, seal it with molten lead and throw it into the Nile. Isis finds the body, so Set cuts it into fourteen pieces and scatters them across Egypt. Isis finds every piece but one, which three fish of the Nile had eaten: the lepidotus, the phagrus and the oxyrhynchus. She makes a replica of it. Wrapped in linen, Osiris becomes the first mummy and lives again, but only as king of the dead. The Pyramid Texts, far older, already tell how Set killed Osiris and how Isis and Nephthys searched for him.

From the Middle Kingdom on, the tomb of King Djer at Abydos was revered as the tomb of Osiris. Pilgrims left so much offering pottery there that the site is still called Umm el-Qa'ab, Arabic for Mother of Pots.

videos.title: Why Did Chang'e Fly to the Moon? | Hou Yi, the Pill of Immortality and Chinese Mythology
videos.description:
A woman swallowed the pill of eternal life, floated up to the Moon, and turned into a toad.

In Chinese myth, ten suns once rose together and scorched the earth, each one carrying a three-legged crow. The archer Hou Yi shot down nine of them and left one. In the Huainanzi, from the Western Han dynasty, Yi asks the Queen Mother of the West for the elixir of immortality, and his wife Chang'e takes it herself and flees to the Moon. In the Lingxian, written by Zhang Heng in the Eastern Han dynasty, she becomes a toad there. Later versions gave her the Guanghan Palace and the jade rabbit that pounds the elixir under the osmanthus tree.

Every Mid-Autumn Festival, millions of people eat mooncakes and look at the Moon for her. China named its lunar exploration program after her: on 3 January 2019, Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon, in Von Karman crater, talking to Earth through the Queqiao relay satellite. Its rover is Yutu-2, the Jade Rabbit. In 2024, Chang'e 6 brought back the first samples from the far side.

videos.title: Why Was Ixion Tied to a Burning Wheel Forever? | Zeus, Hera and Greek Mythology
videos.description:
A king tried to seduce the queen of the gods. So Zeus tied him to a burning wheel that never stops spinning.

Ixion, king of the Lapiths, was remembered as the first man in Greek myth to kill one of his own family: he lured his father-in-law Deioneus to a feast and pushed him into a pit of burning coals hidden under wood and ash. No one would purify him, until Zeus took pity, cleansed him and gave him a seat at the table of the gods. There Ixion wanted Hera. Zeus shaped a cloud in her likeness, later called Nephele, and Ixion lay with it. In Pindar's Second Pythian Ode, the oldest source that links Ixion to the centaurs, their son Centauros fathered the race of centaurs with the mares of Mount Pelion. Pindar binds Ixion to a four-spoked wheel; later writers make it a winged wheel of fire that spins across the sky forever, and later still it turns in Tartarus.

28978 Ixion is a plutino beyond Neptune, about 700 km across, discovered in May 2001 by the Deep Ecliptic Survey at Cerro Tololo and named after the king of the Lapiths.

videos.title: Why Were the Children of Lir Turned Into Swans? | Lir, Aoife and Irish Mythology
videos.description:
A stepmother turned four children into swans for nine hundred years. When the spell broke, they were nine hundred years old.

The Children of Lir (Oidheadh Chlainne Lir) is one of the Three Sorrows of Storytelling in Irish tradition. Lir, of the Tuatha Dé Danann, lost his wife Aobh and married her sister Aoife. Jealous of his love for his four children, Fionnuala, Aodh and the twins Fiachra and Conn, Aoife took them to Lough Derravaragh and with a druid's wand turned them into swans: three hundred years on the lake, three hundred on the Sea of Moyle between Ireland and Scotland, and three hundred at Irrus Domnann (Erris) on the Atlantic. She left them their human voices. Bodb Dearg, king of the Tuatha Dé Danann, punished her by turning her into a demon of the air forever.

At the end of the nine hundred years they heard a Christian bell. When the king Lairgnén seized them, their feathers fell away and they became four withered old people. They were baptised, died, and were buried together.

In Dublin's Garden of Remembrance, Oisín Kelly's bronze Children of Lir, unveiled in 1971, shows the four in the middle of their transformation, their arms turning into wings.

videos.title: Who Was the First Werewolf? | Lycaon, Zeus and Greek Mythology
videos.description:
A king served Zeus a dinner made of human flesh. So Zeus turned him into the first werewolf.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book I), Jupiter tells the gods how he came down to Arcadia disguised as a man. King Lycaon mocked the people who prayed to him and decided to test whether his guest was really a god: he killed a hostage sent by the Molossians, boiled part of the body, roasted the rest and served it. Jupiter brought the house down with his thunderbolt. Lycaon fled into the fields, tried to speak and howled; his clothes turned to fur and his arms to legs, and he became a wolf that kept the same grey hair, the same savage face and the same gleaming eyes.

Pausanias (Description of Greece, VIII 2) gives another version: Lycaon sacrificed a child on the altar of Zeus Lykaios and was turned into a wolf on the spot. Ever since, people said, a man turned into a wolf at every sacrifice there, and became a man again after nine years only if he never tasted human flesh.

In 2016, archaeologists of the Mount Lykaion Excavation and Survey Project found the skeleton of a teenager, about 3,000 years old, buried in Zeus's ash altar on Mount Lykaion. They have not said it was a sacrifice. The name Lycaon comes from lykos, the Greek word for wolf.

videos.title: Why Did Kiyohime Turn Into a Dragon? | Anchin, Dōjō-ji and Japanese Mythology
videos.description:
She chased the monk who lied to her until she became a dragon. Then she cooked him inside a temple bell.

The oldest telling is in the Dainihonkoku Hokekyō kenki, a Buddhist collection from around 1040, and the same story is in the Konjaku monogatarishū, around 1120. A young monk on his way to Kumano spends one night at a house. The woman there falls for him, and he promises to come back only to get away. When she learns he has gone, she chases him, crosses the Hidaka river as a great serpent and finds him at the temple of Dōjō-ji, where the monks have hidden him under the bronze bell. She coils around it and burns him to ash inside.

The names came later: the monk became Anchin in the Genkō shakusho (around 1332) and the woman became Kiyohime on the Edo stage.

By the temple's own account, Dōjō-ji went about four hundred years without a bell, until a new one was given in 1359. That bell was taken to Kyoto and is kept today at Myōman-ji, where its inscription shows it came from Dōjō-ji.

videos.title: Who Really Wrote the Trojan Horse Story? | Virgil, Aeneid, Homer, Greek Mythology
videos.description:
The Trojan Horse story everyone knows was written by the losers.

Homer's Iliad ends with the funeral of Hector, before the horse is built, and the Odyssey only mentions it in passing. The full story, with the priest Laocoon warning "I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts" and the liar Sinon talking the horse through the gates, is book two of the Aeneid. The Roman poet Virgil wrote it some seven hundred years after Homer, and in it the fall of Troy is told by Aeneas, a Trojan prince. Rome claimed Aeneas as its ancestor.

videos.title: Who Made the First Mummy? | Anubis, Osiris and Egyptian Mythology
videos.description:
The first mummy in Egypt was a god.

In the myth of Osiris, his brother Set killed him and cut his body into pieces that were scattered across Egypt. His wife Isis searched until she had found every piece but one. Then Anubis, the god with the head of a jackal, laid the pieces out and wrapped them in linen, and Osiris woke again as king of the dead. Plutarch tells the search in On Isis and Osiris, and the vignettes of the Book of the Dead show Anubis bending over the mummy.

Egyptian priests took his part in the rites of the dead, wearing a jackal mask. A ceramic Anubis mask from the Late Period, with holes for the wearer's eyes, survives in the Roemer- und Pelizaeus-Museum in Hildesheim, Germany.

videos.title: Why Does the Year Have 365 Days? | Thoth, the Moon and Egyptian Mythology
videos.description:
The year has five extra days because a god won them from the Moon.

Plutarch tells it in On Isis and Osiris, chapter 12. The sun god cursed the sky goddess Nut so that she could not give birth in any month of the year. Thoth, the god of wisdom, played the Moon at draughts and won from her the seventieth part of each of her days of light. With it he made five new days outside the 360-day year, and on them Nut gave birth to Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis and Nephthys.

The Egyptian calendar really had twelve months of thirty days and five extra days at the end of the year, and each of those five days was kept as the birthday of one of these gods.

videos.title: What Is Directly Under Your Feet? | Tartarus, Hesiod, the Titans, Greek Myth
videos.description:
A Greek poet measured the underworld by dropping an anvil into it.

He said a bronze anvil falls for nine days and nine nights to get from the sky down to the earth, and for another nine to get from the earth down to the bottom of the world. That bottom is Tartarus: a pit with a gate of bronze and a wall of night wrapped three times around its neck. Inside it are the Titans, the gods who ruled before Zeus and lost the war against him. They are not dead down there. They are kept.

Nine days down, nine days up. The pit is exactly as deep as the sky is high, and we live on the line in the middle.

videos.title: Why Did Horus Feed His Eye to His Dead Father? | Eye of Horus, Set, Osiris, Egyptian Mythology
videos.description:
Horus lost an eye fighting the uncle who murdered his father.

After Set killed Osiris and took the throne of Egypt, Osiris's son Horus claimed it back. In the Contendings of Horus and Set, a papyrus written around 1150 BC, the gods put the case on trial, and it dragged on for eighty years of contests and fights. In one of them Set tore out Horus's eye. In other texts the eye is broken into pieces and the god Thoth puts it back together, and the healed eye is called the wedjat, "the sound one". In the Pyramid Texts, Horus gives that eye to his dead father to eat, and it gives Osiris new life as king of the dead. The wedjat became the most common amulet in ancient Egypt, and it is the Eye of Horus people still wear today.

The trial and the eighty years are in the Contendings of Horus and Set (Papyrus Chester Beatty I); the eye given to Osiris is in the Pyramid Texts.

videos.title: Why Did Ireland's Greatest Hero Keep Biting His Thumb? | Finn McCool, Salmon of Knowledge
videos.description:
He burned his thumb on a fish and knew everything after.

Nine hazel trees stood over a sacred well in Ireland, and their nuts fell into the water. A salmon ate them, and with them everything there is to know. A poet called Finn Eces waited seven years on the bank of the Boyne to catch that salmon, because it had been foretold that whoever ate it would hold all knowledge. He caught it at last and gave it to the boy who served him to cook, with one rule: don't taste it. The skin blistered over the fire, the boy pressed it flat with his thumb and burned himself, and he put the thumb in his mouth without thinking. The seven years went to the boy. He grew up to be Finn McCool, and for the rest of his life, whenever he needed an answer, he bit that thumb.

Odin's missing eye is at the bottom of a well.

In the Prose Edda, under the root of the world tree Yggdrasil that reaches toward the land of the frost giants, there is a well where wisdom and understanding lie hidden. Its keeper is Mimir, and he is wise because he drinks from it every day. Odin came and asked for a single drink, and he did not get it until he left one of his eyes in the well as a pledge. The poem Voluspa adds the strangest part: Mimir drinks mead every morning from the All-father's pledge. It is the same Mimir whose head Odin later kept and consulted.

The well and the pledge are in Gylfaginning 15, in Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda; the morning drink is Voluspa, stanza 28, in the Poetic Edda.

videos.title: Why Did Odysseus Take 20 Years to Get Home? | Life of Odysseus, Cyclops, Sirens, Calypso
videos.description:
Odysseus tried to dodge the Trojan War, and it cost him twenty years.

As a young man he was gashed by a wild boar on Mount Parnassus, and the scar would one day give him away. When the Greeks came to take him to Troy, he pretended to be mad: he put on a felt cap, yoked a horse and an ox to one plough and sowed his field with salt. It did not work. Ten years later the war ended with his idea, the wooden horse. On the way home he blinded the cyclops Polyphemus, had himself tied to the mast to hear the Sirens, and spent seven years on the island of the goddess Calypso, who would not let him leave. When he finally reached Ithaca, in the twentieth year and disguised as an old beggar, the only one who knew him was his dog Argos. The next day he strung the great bow that none of his wife's suitors could bend.

The scar, the cyclops, the Sirens, Calypso, Argos and the bow are in Homer's Odyssey. The fake madness comes from later writers such as Hyginus, and the wooden horse as his plan from Homer and Apollodorus.

videos.title: Why Did Achilles Hide as a Girl? | Odysseus' Trick, Skyros, Greek Mythology
videos.description:
Achilles once hid from a war, dressed as a girl.

His mother, the sea nymph Thetis, knew that if he went to Troy he would die there. So she dressed him as a girl and hid him among the daughters of King Lycomedes on the island of Skyros. The Greeks had been told they could not take Troy without him, and Odysseus came looking. In the version told by Hyginus he arrived as a merchant and laid out gifts: jewellery and clothes for the princesses, with a shield and a spear among them. Then he had a war trumpet sounded outside. The girls ran, and the one who grabbed the weapons was Achilles. Apollodorus and the Roman poet Statius tell the same story. He went to Troy, and died there.

videos.title: Why Did the Norse Gods Throw Axes at Baldur? | Loki, Mistletoe, Norse Mythology
videos.description:
For fun, the Norse gods threw axes at their friend Baldur, and nothing could hurt him.

The story is in the Prose Edda, in the part called Gylfaginning. Baldur, the most loved of the gods, dreamed of his own death. So his mother Frigg made fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, animals, birds, poison and snakes swear never to harm him. After that, the gods' favourite game was to throw spears, axes and stones at him and watch them bounce off.

Loki, disguised as an old woman, asked Frigg if anything had been left out. Only one young shoot growing west of Valhalla, she said: the mistletoe, too young to take the oath. Loki pulled it up, found Baldur's blind brother Hodur standing outside the circle, put the mistletoe in his hand and guided his aim. It went straight through Baldur, and he fell dead.

Kissing under the mistletoe is a much later custom, but it is the same plant.

videos.title: Why Was Osiris Murdered Twice? | Isis, Set, Horus, Egyptian Mythology
videos.description:
Osiris was murdered twice, by the same brother.

Our fullest version is Plutarch's On Isis and Osiris, written around 100 AD. After Set drowned Osiris in a sealed chest, Isis searched until she found the chest at Byblos and brought the body back to Egypt. Set found it while hunting by moonlight, cut Osiris into fourteen pieces and scattered them. Isis went through the marshes in a papyrus boat and found every piece except one, which had been eaten by fish; Plutarch says that is why some Egyptians would not eat the lepidotus, the phagrus or the oxyrhynchus. She made the missing piece herself. In the Egyptian texts she brings Osiris back long enough to conceive their son Horus, and Osiris becomes king of the dead.

Norse mythology's Voluspa, part 3: the countdown to Ragnarok. "Garm bays hard before the Cliff-Cave." In the last part of Völuspá, the end of the world keeps time with a hound's howl. Each time it comes back, the seeress adds the same promise: "Much do I know, and more can see / Of the fate of the gods, the mighty in fight."

This is Episode 3 of our Poetic Edda series: Völuspá, "the seeress's prophecy", Part 3 (Bellows stanzas 44–60). We follow the refrain through the catastrophe: brothers fighting brothers, Heimdall's horn, Odin at Mimir's head, the ship Naglfar, the serpent and the eagle, Surt coming from the south, Odin against the wolf, Vithar's revenge, Thor's nine steps, the sun turning black, and a green earth rising again where the gods meet at Ithavoll. And we count how many times the hound howls in each manuscript, because the Codex Regius, Guðni Jónsson's edition and Hauksbók don't agree. Which myth should we tell next? Tell us in the comments.

The seeress who speaks for Odin remembers the giants who raised her and the time before anything existed. She tells how the sons of Bur raised Midgard out of the void, how the gods sat in council and named night and morning, and how they spent a golden age at Ithavoll. Then come the dwarfs, Ask and Embla found lifeless on a shore, the ash Yggdrasil and the Norns at its well. And then a woman called Gollveig is struck with spears and burned in Odin's hall. Three times. She comes back every time, and the first war in Norse myth begins: the Aesir against the Vanir, a shattered wall, and oaths the gods break when a giant demands Freyja as his price.

videos.title: Did a Real Volcano Inspire Ragnarok? Iceland's Eldgja Eruption
videos.description:
Did a real volcano inspire Ragnarok? Iceland's Eldgja eruption of around 939, the poem Voluspa and the evidence for a Norse end of the world seen with real eyes.

Around 939, the ground in southern Iceland split open along a crack some seventy-five kilometres long. A few decades later, a poem described the end of the world: the sun turns black, the earth sinks into the sea, steam rises and fire leaps against heaven. Were the Norse imagining something they had actually seen? We look at Völuspá, the Greenland ice-core layers behind the redating of Eldgjá, the tree rings that show the cooling, the lava cave named after the fire giant Surtr where people burned offerings, an argument about angry gods at the Althing in the year 1000, the volcanic winter of 536 and Fimbulwinter, and the birth of Surtsey in 1963. And we are careful about where the evidence stops.

videos.description:
Would you climb into a golden box at a party? One king did, and it cost him his life.

Osiris was the first king of Egypt, and his brother Set wanted his throne. Set secretly measured his brother's body, built a beautiful golden chest that fit those exact measurements, and threw a party with 72 of his friends. Whoever fit inside perfectly could keep the chest. Too tall. Too short. Too wide. Then Osiris lay down, and it was perfect.

Set and his friends slammed the lid, sealed it with melted lead and threw it into the Nile. The king of Egypt was dead, and Set took his throne. But that was only the beginning.

After death, every Egyptian travelled to the hall of Osiris, the king of the dead. There, Anubis put your heart on a scale. On the other side lay a single feather, the feather of truth. A light heart meant paradise: the Fields of Reeds, forever. A heart heavy with bad deeds was eaten by Ammit, part crocodile, part lion, part hippo, and you were gone forever.

The question was never how powerful you were. It was how heavy your heart is. Would yours pass?

videos.title: A Fish Ate Part Of A God 🐟 #shorts #egyptianmythology #mythology
videos.description:
The first mummy in history was missing one piece, and a fish ate it.

When the god Osiris was murdered by his jealous brother Set, his body was cut into 14 pieces and scattered across Egypt. His wife Isis and her sister Nephthys built a boat out of papyrus and searched the entire Nile, piece by piece. They found 13. The 14th had been eaten by a fish, and in some places Egyptians refused to eat those fish for centuries.

With the help of Anubis, the jackal god, they put Osiris back together and wrapped him in linen from head to toe. That's how the first mummy was made, according to Egyptian myth.

Watch the full story of Osiris, Isis, Set and Horus in "The ENTIRE Story of Egyptian Mythology" on the channel.

Source: Plutarch, "On Isis and Osiris".

Roman army hospital, the valetudinarium, and the world's first hospitals: inside the Roman military hospital system that treated legionaries centuries before any civilian had a ward.

Behind the walls of every Roman fortress stood a building no civilian could buy a bed in: two rows of wards around a courtyard, doctors on the payroll, walls built thick for quiet, and a surgeon with an instrument designed for one impossible job. In this video we walk through its doors, meet the stretcher men who ran toward the wounded under arrow fire, read the morning list that counted one garrison's damage man by man, and stand at the operating table where a barbed arrowhead met the spoon of Diocles.

Why did an empire that spent men like water on its frontiers spend silver putting them back together? The building itself is the clue.

videos.title: What Did a Roman Soldier Actually Eat?
videos.description:
Roman Soldier Food — What Did a Roman Soldier Actually Eat? | Roman army food, legionary rations, army pay deductions and the barley punishment

Rome paid its soldiers in wheat, charged them for the wheat, and made them grind it themselves. This is the real Roman army food story, weighed out one dinner at a time: about 850 grams of whole wheat a day, a pay slip from the siege of Masada where the deductions ate an entire wage, eight men sharing one tent and one hand mill, biscuit you had to soak before it would soften, sour wine in every cup, and an emperor who made a point of eating bacon, cheese and that same sour wine in front of his men.

Then there is the dark side of the menu. Barley was horse food, and Rome fed it to men as a punishment. At one British fort, the rubbish pits and ink tablets preserve 46 different foodstuffs, and a cavalry officer's exasperated letter home about the beer. And when the wheat ran out on campaign in the east, the price of bread did something no soldier could afford.

Which surprises you more: that the army deducted the food from the soldier's own pay, or that barley counted as a punishment? Tell us in the comments.

samanid empire — the entire history of the samanid empire and the samanid dynasty, explained: how a forgotten Persian empire brought the Persian language back from the dead.

In the year 800, the Persian language was dying in public. Millions still spoke it in villages and kitchens, but no king wrote it and no court paid a poet to sing in it. Then four brothers from a family of Persian landowners were handed four cities — and the Samanid Empire they built over the next 180 years, ruling Transoxiana from Bukhara, would spend its power on something no conqueror had ever bought before: bringing a language back from the dead. Under Ismail Samani, the empire's founder, its armies held the steppe frontier, its roads were so safe that frontier towns let their walls decay, and its silver dirhams travelled so far north that they are still being dug out of Viking hoards in Sweden today.

At its height, Bukhara was a rival of Baghdad: its colleges crowded with jurists, astronomers and physicians, its book market fed by the famous paper of Samarkand. Here the blind poet Rudaki made Persian a language of high art again, here Ferdowsi's Shahnameh — fifty thousand verses — was begun, and here a teenage boy named Avicenna talked his way into the royal library and taught himself the medicine his Canon would teach Europe for six hundred years. videos.title: The Dancing Plague of 1518: History's Strangest Epidemic
videos.description:
One woman started dancing in July 1518, and she could not stop. Within weeks, hundreds of people in Strasbourg had joined her, dancing day and night until their feet bled and their bodies gave out. This is the true story of the dancing plague of 1518, the strangest medieval epidemic ever recorded — an outbreak no doctor could explain and no law could end.

The woman's name was Frau Troffea, and she began in a city already on the edge. Strasbourg in 1518 was hungry, frightened and half-convinced the world was ending: famine had emptied the granaries, disease moved through the crowded streets, and everyone knew the old stories about the curse of Saint Vitus, the saint who could condemn a sinner to dance without rest. When Frau Troffea's feet started moving and would not stop, the city did not see an illness. It saw a curse taking hold — and then, one by one, her neighbours started dancing too.

The doctors who examined the dancers gave the medieval epidemic a diagnosis that sounds like a joke today: hot blood. And their prescription was worse. The only cure, they said, was more dancing — so the city council cleared a hall, built a stage in the market square and hired musicians to keep the music going around the clock. It was, in effect, a government rave for people who were dying on their feet. videos.title: The Cadaver Synod: When the Church Put a Dead Pope on Trial
videos.description:
In January 897, a pope in Rome ordered a grave opened. The man inside, Pope Formosus, had been dead for nine months — but that did not save him. His corpse was washed, dressed in papal robes, propped upright on a throne in the Lateran Basilica, and put on trial by his successor, Pope Stephen VI, on three charges: perjury, ambition, and breaking canon law. This is the Cadaver Synod, the strangest trial in history, and the true story of the day the medieval Church put a dead pope on trial.

Formosus had lived a life that made powerful enemies. A brilliant bishop who was excommunicated by one pope, forgiven by another, and finally elected pope himself in 891, he played a dangerous double game between two kings fighting for Italy — crowning Guy of Spoleto emperor, then secretly inviting Arnulf of Carinthia to invade and rescue him. When Formosus died in April 896, he was buried with honour in Saint Peter's Basilica. But his enemies in the Spoleto faction had not forgotten, and when Stephen VI took the throne, revenge came with him. Stephen had his own secret, too: Formosus had ordained him bishop, so if Formosus could be declared never to have been pope at all, Stephen's own rise could never be challenged.

videos.title: Every God in Egyptian Mythology Explained
videos.description:
Egypt worshipped more gods than any civilization in history — by modern count, around fifteen hundred of them, across three thousand years. This is every major god in Egyptian mythology explained: Ra, who sails across the sky in his solar boat and fights a giant serpent every single night; Amun, the hidden god whose priests grew richer than kings; Osiris, the murdered king who became ruler of the dead; Isis, the goddess who outwitted the sun himself; and Seth, Horus, Anubis, Thoth, Hathor, Sekhmet, Bastet, Sobek and Khepri — ending with Apophis, the one god all of Egypt prayed would lose.

But look closer, and a pattern appears. Almost everything these gods do is about a single enemy: death. The sun dies every evening and is reborn every morning. The murdered king does not stay dead — he wakes up ruling the afterlife. Every human heart is weighed against one feather, and the prize for passing is a paradise of green fields. Ancient Egyptian religion was the ancient world's most determined refusal to accept that the dead have to stay dead, and this video explains how the whole extraordinary machine worked, god by god.

We are honest about the evidence, too: Egypt never had one single canon, the famous count of fifteen hundred gods is a modern reconstruction, and some of the best-loved stories survive only in late sources like Plutarch. videos.title: Your Life as Every Ottoman Janissary Rank
videos.description:
You are eight years old when the Sultan's men take you from your village — and that kidnapping is the start of the strangest military career in Ottoman Empire history. This is your life as a janissary, rank by rank, from a stolen Balkan child in the devshirme child levy to the supreme commander of the most feared infantry corps in the world.

The janissaries were the elite soldiers of the Ottoman army: Christian boys taken from their families, converted, and forged through years of brutal training into professional musketeers, centuries before Europe had standing armies. In this animated history story, you climb the entire ladder of janissary ranks yourself. You begin as an acemi oglan, a raw cadet hauling stone and rowing the Sultan's galleys, before taking the oath and earning the tall bork cap of a full yeniceri. Then the promotions begin: onbashi, leader of ten men. Oda bashi, chief of your barracks chamber. And then corbaci — literally "the soup server" — commander of your orta, whose rank badge was a spoon and whose authority flowed from a giant copper soup cauldron called the kazan.

Because in the Ottoman Empire, soup was power. Janissaries were paid a real salary every three months, fed from the Sultan's own kitchen, and loyal to their cauldron the way other armies are loyal to a flag. videos.title: Saturn the Greater Malefic: Planetary Magic in the Grimoire Tradition
videos.description:
Ptolemy called it the greater malefic. Cold, dry, distant, the slowest thing the naked eye could track against the fixed stars -- and for the next fourteen hundred years, nobody practicing astrology treated that as a metaphor.

A real, technical literature grew out of it. The Picatrix told a magician exactly what to carve, in what metal, at what hour, to work with Saturn rather than simply suffer it. Agrippa gave the planet a number: a nine-cell grid where every row, column and diagonal sums to fifteen. A ninth century Baghdad philosopher explained why any of it should work at all. A Dominican friar wrote a formal objection to the whole premise. None of this is speculation -- it's documented, cross-referenced, and it's where the black cube's color and reputation actually come from, minus everything that made it a discipline.

One case study runs through the middle of it. Marsilio Ficino was born with Saturn dominant in his own chart -- a diagnosis that, in 1480, meant something close to a life sentence. He didn't argue with the astrology. He used it, and wrote a book explaining how.

videos.title: The Universe's Ultimate Speed Limit 🚀

Mind-bending twist: space itself has no speed limit. The universe is expanding, and distant galaxies are moving away from us faster than light. That doesn't break Einstein's rule, because it's space stretching, not objects moving through it. 🌌

videos.title: Why Do We Forget Our Dreams? 🧠💤
videos.description:
You wake up with a vivid dream… and 30 seconds later it's gone. Why? 🧠

During REM sleep, your brain is busy dreaming, but the chemicals and brain regions that save memories are mostly switched off. Noradrenaline, the "save this" signal, drops very low, and the hippocampus isn't writing your dreams into long-term memory. Some research even suggests certain neurons actively help erase them.

So the dream was real while it lasted. Your brain just never hit "save." 💾

Tip: keep a notebook by your bed and write it down the second you wake up, before you move.

videos.title: Ragnarok: How the Norse Sagas Said the World Would End, Step by Step
videos.description:
Ragnarok, step by step: how the Norse end of the world unfolds in the surviving sources, from the three-year Fimbulwinter to Fenrir, Jormungandr, Surtr's fire and the people who come out the other side.

We follow the order given in the Poetic Edda and in Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, and we flag where they disagree.

We also cover the part most retellings skip. These texts were written down in Christian Iceland in the 1200s, long after the conversion, so scholars still debate how much reflects older belief and how much was reshaped later.

videos.title: Tiamat Made 11 Monsters to Kill the Gods. One Now Guards a Museum
videos.description:
Tiamat's 11 monsters from the Enuma Elish, the Babylonian creation epic: every one of them, what it looked like, and what happened to it after the gods won.

More than three thousand years ago, a Babylonian poem told how Tiamat, the primordial sea, built an army of eleven monsters to kill the gods. The gods sent their strongest, and they turned back. Then the young god Marduk stood up.

We meet all eleven one by one, from Bashmu the horned serpent to Kusarikku the bull man, follow the battle between Marduk and Tiamat, and end with the strangest part of the story: the monsters did not disappear. They became guardians. Clay figures of them were buried under the floors of ancient houses, and one of them, the dragon Mushhushshu, still stands in blue glazed brick on the Ishtar Gate, rebuilt in a museum in Berlin.

This superboss is the embodiment of Drowning, but if you manage to defeat it, you can fully breath underwater in Look Outside. videos.title: What Did Jesus Mean by "The Kingdom of God Is Within You"? | Luke 17:21 Explained
videos.description:
Jesus once said, "The kingdom of God is within you." But here's something interesting: He was speaking to the Pharisees, the very people asking when God's kingdom would come.

So what did He actually mean?

In Luke 17:20–21, Jesus gives an answer that's easy to misunderstand. Some Bible translations say the kingdom is "within you," while others say "among you" or "in your midst." And when you look at the people He was speaking to, that difference becomes surprisingly important.

In this video, we'll look at the world Jesus lived in, what people expected God's kingdom to look like, why His answer was so unexpected, and how His words connect to what He taught about the future coming of the Son of Man.

It's a short passage, but there's much more behind it than it first appears.

Chapters:
00:00 – The Kingdom of God Is Within You?
02:10 – The Kingdom They Were Waiting For
05:26 – The Kingdom Was Already Among Them
09:43 – Within You or Among You?
14:14 – If the Kingdom Was Already Here, Why Would It Come Again?
17:58 – What This Means for Us Today

Scripture references: Luke 17:20–37, Daniel 7:13–14, Luke 11:20, Matthew 23:26, Romans 14:17.

#BibleExplained #Luke1721 #KingdomOfGod

videos.title: 12 Tribes of Israel Explained — What Made Each One Different
videos.description:
Israel had twelve tribes, but their stories were anything but identical.

Reuben was the firstborn, yet he lost his birthright. Levi received no separate tribal territory. Judah became the royal line, while Joseph's two sons were given their own tribal inheritances.

And when you compare the different lists of the twelve tribes in the Bible, something even more interesting happens. Some names change, others disappear, and the order isn't always the same.

In this video, we'll look at what made each tribe different, the roles they played in Israel's history, and why the twelve tribes still appear in the book of Revelation.

**Chapters:**

00:00 – Why the Twelve Tribes Don't Always Match
02:05 – Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah
06:16 – Joseph's Double Inheritance and Benjamin
09:50 – The Tribes History Often Overlooks
13:43 – Gad, Dan, and the Divided Kingdom
17:52 – The Twelve Tribes in Revelation

Scripture references include Genesis 35, 44, 48–49; Numbers 32; Joshua 13–19; Judges 18; 1 Chronicles 5 and 12; Isaiah 9; Matthew 4; Luke 2; and Revelation 7 and 21.

#12TribesOfIsrael #BibleExplained #BibleStudy

videos.title: The Parable of the Unjust Steward Explained | Luke 16
videos.description:
Why would a dishonest manager receive praise instead of punishment? In Luke 16, Jesus tells a strange story about a man who is about to lose his job and decides to reduce the debts owed to his master. What happens next is probably not what you'd expect.

The Parable of the Unjust Steward has puzzled readers for centuries. Was Jesus really praising dishonesty? What did He mean by making friends with worldly wealth? And how does this unusual story lead to His warning that no one can serve both God and money?

We'll walk through the story, explain the confusing parts, and explore what Jesus was teaching about wisdom, money, faithfulness, and preparing for the future.

01:29 A MANAGER ABOUT TO LOSE EVERYTHING.
05:02 WHY WAS A DISHONEST MAN PRAISED.
09:20 WHAT DOES “MAKE FRIENDS WITH MONEY” MEAN.
13:15 THE REAL LESSON ABOUT MONEY AND FAITHFULNESS.
17:14 WHAT THIS PARABLE MEANS FOR US TODAY.

#BibleExplained #ParablesOfJesus #Luke16

videos.title: Every Miracle Jesus Performed on the Sabbath Explained
videos.description:
Jesus healed a man who had been sick for 38 years. But instead of celebrating, some religious leaders questioned why he was carrying his mat on the Sabbath.

And that wasn't the only time a healing caused trouble.

Jesus restored a man's withered hand, healed a woman who had been bent over for 18 years, gave sight to a man born blind, and performed several other miracles on the Sabbath. Some people were amazed. Others were convinced He was doing something wrong.

So what was the problem with healing on the Sabbath? Was Jesus actually breaking God's law? And why did He call Himself the Lord of the Sabbath?

We'll go through seven miracles recorded in the Gospels, look at what happened in each one, and try to understand why something as wonderful as healing a sick person could become such a serious controversy.

**Bible passages:** John 5:1–18, John 9, Mark 1:21–34, Mark 3:1–6, Luke 6:6–11, Luke 13:10–17, Luke 14:1–6, Matthew 12:9–14.

Timestamps
00:00 The Man Who Waited 38 Years.
02:52 The Man with the Withered Hand.
05:24 The Woman Bent Over for 18 Years.
07:57 The Man Born Blind.

videos.title: Every Name of God in the Bible and What They Mean
videos.description:
Why does the Bible call God Yahweh, Jehovah, Elohim, El Shaddai, and so many other names? Are they all names for the same God, or do they mean different things?

There's actually a lot more behind these names than most people realize. For example, the word LORD in many English Bibles is often standing in for God's personal name, YHWH. And some familiar names, like Jehovah Jireh and Jehovah Shalom, originally came from specific events in the Old Testament.

In this video, we'll break down the most important names of God in the Bible, explain their Hebrew and Greek meanings, and look at the stories behind them.

We'll also explore names and titles like El Roi, Adonai, the Ancient of Days, Immanuel, and Alpha and Omega, including how the New Testament connects some of these ideas to Jesus.

Some are personal names. Others are titles, descriptions, or names given to places. Understanding the difference helps make sense of passages that can otherwise be confusing.

videos.title: 5 Lies God Wants to Tear Down in Your Mind
videos.description:
Some of the most limiting lies do not sound negative. They sound reasonable, familiar, and even wise. You may believe you cannot change, that your strongest feelings must be true, or that you need every answer before you can have peace.

In this encouraging biblical message, we uncover five subtle lies that can quietly shape your thoughts, delay your obedience, and keep you from recognizing what God is already doing in your life. Through Scripture and practical examples, you will learn how God renews your mind, replaces fear with truth, and helps you see growth even when progress seems hidden.

You do not need to become someone else before God can use you. You can begin today with the faith, gifts, opportunities, and small acts of obedience already in your hands. Let God’s truth have the final word over your identity, your future, and the way you see your life.

Timestamps:
00:00 Introduction.
01:26 Part 1. The Lie That Says, I Have Always Been This Way, So I Will Never Change.
04:28 Part 2. The Lie That Says, The Loudest Thought in My Mind Must Be True.
07:25 Part 3. The Lie That Says, I Must Understand and Control Everything Before I Can Have Peace.
10:21 Part 4. The Lie That Says, If I Cannot See Progress, God Must Not Be Doing Anything.
13:16 Part 5. The Lie That Says, God Will Use Me When I Become a Better Version of Myself.
16:14 Conclusion.

#GodsTruth #RenewYourMind #ChristianEncouragement #FaithInGod #BiblicalWisdom
tags: God is working in your life

videos.title: 5 Things People Say When God Begins to Change You
videos.description:
When God begins to change you, the people around you may notice it before you do. They hear it in the way you speak, see it in the way you respond, and recognize that the things which once controlled you are beginning to lose their power.

Some may say, “You seem different lately.” Others may wonder why you no longer enjoy the same conversations, habits, or approval you once needed. Your new boundaries may be misunderstood as pride, while your growing peace may cause someone to ask what happened to you.

In this biblical message, we will explore five things people often say when God begins transforming your heart. You will discover how the renewing of your mind changes your reactions, desires, relationships, boundaries, and everyday choices. You will also learn how to remain humble, loving, and faithful when others do not immediately understand what God is doing within you.

God’s deepest work often begins quietly, through one prayer, one surrendered response, and one small act of obedience at a time. You do not have to announce your transformation. Let the fruit of the Holy Spirit speak through your peace, patience, faithfulness, and love.

Timestamps:

07:23 Part 3. You Think You Are Better Than Us.

15:58 Conclusion.

#GodIsChangingYo

videos.title: 5 People God May Be Warning You to Walk Away From
videos.description:
Not every difficult relationship is one God is asking you to end. But some people consistently distract you from your purpose, take without giving, weaken your confidence, avoid responsibility, or use their words to create division.

In this biblical message, we will look at five kinds of people God may be warning you to step away from. This is not about hatred, bitterness, or judging others. It is about discernment, healthy boundaries, spiritual growth, and protecting what God is building in your life.

You can forgive someone without restoring the same access. You can love people without allowing them to control your time, peace, decisions, and relationship with God. Ask the Holy Spirit for wisdom, and trust Him to show you when patience is needed, when an honest conversation is needed, and when it is time to move forward.

videos.title: The WORST Copycats of Popular Superheroes
videos.description:
Two universes. Sixty years of "wait… haven't I seen this before?"

We look at every major case where Marvel and DC copied, borrowed, or accidentally reinvented each other's biggest ideas — the cosmic warlords, the teams of outcasts led by a genius in a wheelchair, the superhero zombie apocalypses, and the two funerals that stopped the entire comic industry in its tracks. videos.title: WHY The Avengers Never Recruited More Members EXPLAINED
videos.description:
Ever wonder why the Avengers' movie roster looks nothing like the comics?

This video breaks down the real reason the MCU stuck to a tight, six-hero core instead of the massive, ever-rotating roster fans know from the comics, and it's not just a creative choice. 

We dig into the legal chaos of Marvel's near-bankruptcy in the 90s, the sell-off of character rights to Sony, Fox, and Universal, and how that left Kevin Feige and Marvel Studios working with what Hollywood considered the leftovers. 

From the Hulk's bizarre distribution rights situation, to the Maximoff twins' mutant identity being legally erased, to the insane $71.3 billion Disney-Fox acquisition that finally cleared the path for mutants to enter the MCU, this is the untold business and legal history behind why characters like Wolverine, the Fantastic Four, and dozens of comic-accurate Avengers were kept off screen for over a decade. 

We also look at Joss Whedon's struggle to balance the original six, the scrapped early drafts involving the Wasp, and just how close the entire franchise came to never existing in the first place. 

So was it all a brilliant creative strategy, or did Marvel simply have no other option? Watch until the end to find out exactly how deep this rabbit hole goes.

videos.title: Superhero's That Actually EXIST in Real Life
videos.description:

We're talking super strength, wall-climbing, regeneration, invisibility, and the actual biology, physics, and chemistry that explain how close (or far) humans and animals really are from having these powers for real.

Geckos, axolotls, cuttlefish, glass frogs, Van der Waals forces, blastemas, active camouflage, echolocation, it's all in here, and it's all real. Marvel fans, science nerds, and anyone who's ever wondered "could this actually happen?" need to see this.

We break down the Titan battle beat by beat as a duel of adaptation rather than raw power, the Mark 50 nanotech suit as a problem-solving engine, and the moment a man in a metal suit did something to a being holding four Infinity Stones that no one else managed.

videos.title: Why Thanos REFUSED to Double the Universe's Resources?

Everyone's asked it. With the Reality Stone in his grip, why didn't Thanos just double the universe's resources instead of wiping out half of all life?

Turns out the answer has nothing to do with the Infinity Stones and everything to do with what's going on inside Thanos's head. In this deep dive, we're unpacking the real psychology behind the Snap using direct quotes and interviews from the Russo Brothers, screenwriters Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, and Kevin Feige himself, breaking down the Mad Titan's messiah complex, his obsession with being proven right, and why the so-called "plot hole" everyone complains about is actually one of the most consistent character decisions in the entire MCU.

We're going planet by planet, stone by stone, through the logistics of what doubling resources would actually require, the resource wars it could trigger, the chaos of cosmic micromanagement, and why Thanos was never built to be the guy who solves a problem cleanly. 

We also dig into why the comics version of Thanos might be more honest than his movie counterpart, and how the math behind the Snap exposes a hypocrisy buried right in the heart of the Mad Titan's plan. If you've ever wondered why the smartest villain in the MCU made what looks like the dumbest possible choice, stick around, because the real answer is way darker than a plot hole.
